territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: At a fixed annotation budget, labeling a few slices in many patients beats densely labeling few patients for 3D organ segmentation.
problem: Annotation budgets for 3D medical segmentation are spent by convention on dense per-volume masks, without evidence that this allocation maximizes downstream accuracy.
core_hypothesis: Inter-patient anatomical and acquisition variability contributes more to generalization error than intra-volume slice redundancy, so spreading sparse slice labels across more patients yields better models per annotation-hour.
falsifiable_prediction: Under a matched annotator-hour budget, a model trained on k sparsely labeled slices per volume across N patients will outperform a model trained on dense masks for the equivalent smaller patient count, with the gap growing as patient diversity increases.
why_important: Annotation cost is the dominant bottleneck in clinical segmentation projects; a validated budget-allocation rule would change how labeling campaigns are designed.
why_possibly_novel: Sparse-label training methods exist, but a controlled annotation-economics study that holds annotator time constant and varies the patients-vs-slices allocation appears under-examined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one public multi-organ CT dataset, simulate budgets by subsampling slices vs subsampling patients at equal estimated labeling time, train identical architectures, and compare test Dice and surface distance across budget levels with multiple seeds.
main_risk: Slice-level labeling time may not scale linearly with slice count, making the budget equivalence assumption contestable and the result sensitive to the time model.
community_default_belief: Dense volumetric masks are the gold standard and partial labels are a degraded fallback used only when budgets are tight.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adjacent slices are highly correlated so their marginal information is small, while each new patient contributes independent anatomy, pathology, and scanner variation the model has never seen.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One-day run: train two models at a single matched budget (sparse-many-patients vs dense-few-patients) on an existing labeled dataset by masking labels, and check whether the sparse-allocation model is at least on par.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Two orthogonal-plane scribbles per structure recover most of dense-mask supervision for 3D organ segmentation.
problem: Scribble supervision is usually evaluated on 2D or with ad hoc scribble placement, so it is unclear what minimal 3D scribble protocol clinicians should actually follow.
core_hypothesis: A standardized protocol of one axial plus one coronal or sagittal scribble per structure constrains 3D extent well enough that consistency-regularized training closes most of the gap to full masks.
falsifiable_prediction: A fixed two-orthogonal-scribble protocol will retain a large majority of full-supervision Dice on abdominal organs, while single-plane scribbles of equal total length will retain substantially less.
why_important: A concrete, minimal annotation protocol is directly actionable for hospitals building in-house models and reduces labeling cost by an order of magnitude if it holds.
why_possibly_novel: Scribble-supervised medical segmentation is studied, but protocol-level questions (how many planes, which orientations, standardized placement) framed as a prescriptive annotation standard appear less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate scribbles from existing dense labels under several plane protocols on a public abdominal CT set, train a scribble-supervised baseline for each protocol, and compare Dice retention curves.
main_risk: Simulated scribbles may not reflect real annotator behavior, so a positive simulation result may not transfer to genuine annotation sessions.
community_default_belief: Weak labels trade accuracy for cost roughly proportionally, and dense masks remain necessary for high-stakes structures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: 3D shape priors and unlabeled-voxel consistency losses supply most missing constraints, so the marginal value of dense labels beyond a well-placed skeleton of scribbles may be small.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Half-day run: convert labels of a small organ dataset into orthogonal scribbles, fine-tune an existing scribble-supervised pipeline, and check whether Dice retention is far above the single-plane control.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Mine radiology report phrases for lesion location and laterality as weak supervision to train lesion segmentation without pixel labels.
problem: Hospitals hold huge archives of imaging with narrative reports but almost no pixel-level lesion annotations.
core_hypothesis: Structured facts extractable from reports (organ, laterality, approximate size, count) impose enough spatial constraints that a constraint-based loss can train a usable lesion segmenter from otherwise unlabeled scans.
falsifiable_prediction: A model trained only with report-derived constraints on unlabeled scans will localize a majority of lesions found by a fully supervised model on the same test set, and adding a small labeled seed set will close most of the remaining gap.
why_important: It converts existing clinical archives into training signal, sidestepping the annotation bottleneck for lesion tasks where labeling is most expensive.
why_possibly_novel: Report-supervised classification is common; converting report facts into differentiable spatial constraints for volumetric lesion segmentation appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset that has both reports and lesion masks, strip the masks, extract structured facts with an NLP pipeline, train with constraint losses (count, organ region, size bounds), and evaluate against held-out masks.
main_risk: Report extraction noise and vague spatial language may make constraints too loose, leading the model to satisfy constraints with anatomically plausible but wrong regions.
community_default_belief: Pixel-level lesion segmentation requires at least some pixel-level ground truth; reports are only useful for image-level classification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Lesions are conspicuous local anomalies, so weak constraints plus an anomaly-sensitive image prior may suffice to pin them down without explicit masks.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Quick test on one organ: use only lesion count and organ constraints from existing metadata, train briefly, and check whether lesion-level recall is meaningfully above an unsupervised anomaly-detection baseline.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Anatomy-shaped masking for masked-image pretraining: corrupt organ-shaped regions instead of random patches to pretrain segmentation encoders.
problem: Generic masked image modeling ignores that downstream medical segmentation targets are contiguous anatomical shapes, potentially wasting pretraining signal.
core_hypothesis: Reconstructing anatomy-shaped occlusions forces the encoder to learn organ boundary and context cues that transfer better to segmentation than square-patch masking.
falsifiable_prediction: With pretraining data and compute matched, anatomy-shaped masking will beat random-patch masking on few-label downstream segmentation, with the advantage concentrated in boundary metrics rather than region overlap.
why_important: Self-supervised pretraining is the main lever when labels are scarce, and a masking strategy is nearly free to change.
why_possibly_novel: Masking-strategy ablations exist in the natural-image literature; deriving mask shapes from coarse anatomical atlases or registration priors specifically for medical segmentation transfer appears under-examined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain twin encoders on unlabeled CT with random-patch vs atlas-shaped masks, fine-tune both on small labeled subsets of an organ dataset, and compare Dice and surface distance across label fractions.
main_risk: Masked-region shape may matter far less than mask ratio and data scale, yielding a null result indistinguishable from noise across seeds.
community_default_belief: Masked image modeling is shape-agnostic; what matters is masking ratio, data volume, and encoder capacity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In medical images the label structure is strongly tied to specific shapes and boundaries, so aligning the pretext corruption with the downstream output distribution could matter more than in natural images.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Short pretraining runs (limited epochs) with both masking schemes on a subset of unlabeled volumes, then linear-probe-style decoding on a labeled set to compare early transfer signal.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Single-atlas registration propagation plus learned shape-plausibility filtering as a pseudo-label engine that rivals small supervised training sets.
problem: Classical atlas-based segmentation is dismissed as obsolete, yet it produces spatially coherent labels without any training data, which modern pipelines could exploit.
core_hypothesis: Registration-propagated labels filtered by a shape-plausibility scorer give pseudo-labels whose quality-per-cost exceeds training on the small manually labeled sets typical of new clinical projects.
falsifiable_prediction: A network trained on filtered atlas-propagated pseudo-labels from unlabeled volumes will match or exceed a network trained on a small number of manual volumes for large stable organs, though not for lesions.
why_important: It offers a zero-annotation cold-start recipe for new sites and anatomies, which matters for the long tail of structures with no public labels.
why_possibly_novel: Atlas methods and pseudo-labeling are both old; the specific combination with a learned per-region plausibility filter as a cold-start protocol, evaluated against equivalent manual-label budgets, appears rarely quantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public abdominal dataset, hold out all labels except one atlas volume, generate propagated pseudo-labels across the unlabeled pool, filter, train, and compare with models trained on 3, 5, 10 manual volumes.
main_risk: Registration failures on atypical anatomy could poison pseudo-labels in exactly the cases where a model is clinically most needed.
community_default_belief: Deep networks trained on even small labeled sets dominate atlas-based methods, which are considered legacy technology.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The comparison is usually made at fixed data, not fixed cost; at true zero-annotation cost the atlas pipeline provides thousands of imperfect labels whose aggregate signal may beat a handful of perfect ones.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Propagate one atlas across a modest unlabeled pool with an off-the-shelf registration tool, train a lightweight network on the raw pseudo-labels, and check whether test Dice on large organs approaches the few-manual-volume baseline.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Active learning that queries individual structures within a volume instead of whole volumes yields better accuracy per annotator-hour.
problem: Volume-level active learning forces annotators to label everything in a selected scan, even structures the model already segments well.
core_hypothesis: Model uncertainty is structure-specific, so directing annotation to the specific organ-scan pairs with highest expected error reduction dominates whole-volume selection at equal cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Structure-level acquisition will reach a target mean Dice with substantially fewer annotator-hours than volume-level acquisition, with the largest savings on multi-organ tasks where per-structure difficulty is heterogeneous.
why_important: Active learning is widely piloted in medical annotation tooling, and the query granularity decision affects every labeling campaign built on it.
why_possibly_novel: Active learning for segmentation is well studied at image and region granularity; framing acquisition at the semantic-structure level with per-structure cost models in 3D medical volumes appears less developed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate active learning on a fully labeled multi-organ dataset, comparing volume-level vs structure-level acquisition under a per-structure labeling-time model, tracking Dice vs cumulative simulated hours.
main_risk: Context effects: annotators may label a second organ in an open scan much faster than the cost model assumes, eroding the simulated advantage.
community_default_belief: The scan is the natural unit of annotation work, and switching scans mid-campaign is where the real cost lies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern annotation tools amortize scan loading well, and per-structure difficulty differences (small or low-contrast organs) are large enough to reward targeted queries.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One simulation sweep on an existing labeled dataset with a plausible time model; if structure-level acquisition shows no cost advantage even under favorable assumptions, the idea dies.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Pay annotators to refine model-proposed boundaries only where a disagreement detector flags them, and measure Dice-per-dollar against de novo masking.
problem: Correction-based annotation is assumed cheaper than drawing from scratch, but anchoring bias means annotators may accept wrong proposals, and the economics are rarely measured.
core_hypothesis: Targeted refinement guided by a model-disagreement detector yields more accuracy improvement per unit annotator time than both full de novo annotation and unguided correction, while limiting anchoring-induced label bias.
falsifiable_prediction: In a controlled annotation study, guided refinement will produce training labels that give higher downstream Dice per annotator-hour than de novo masks, and labels from unguided correction will show measurable anchoring bias toward model errors.
why_important: Almost all industrial medical labeling now starts from model proposals; quantifying and mitigating anchoring directly affects dataset quality everywhere.
why_possibly_novel: Model-assisted annotation is standard practice, but jointly measuring the economics and the anchoring-bias cost, with a flagging mechanism as the mitigation, appears under-studied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recruit annotators to label the same volumes under three conditions (de novo, unguided correction, flag-guided correction), time each, train models on each label set, and compare downstream accuracy and label bias against expert consensus.
main_risk: Requires a real annotation study with multiple annotators, which is logistically heavier than purely computational experiments.
community_default_belief: Correcting model outputs is strictly cheaper and label quality is unaffected as long as annotators are instructed to fix errors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Anchoring is a robust cognitive bias; annotators systematically under-correct plausible-looking proposals, silently injecting model errors into the ground truth.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Small pilot with two annotators on a handful of volumes measuring correction acceptance rates against a blinded expert reference to confirm or refute anchoring before scaling the study.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Physics-consistent lesion pasting: synthesize rare-class lesions by intensity-model-based blending into healthy scans rather than GAN synthesis.
problem: Rare lesion classes have too few examples to train segmenters, and generative synthesis pipelines are heavy, hard to validate, and can hallucinate.
core_hypothesis: Simple copy-paste of real lesion patches with modality-aware intensity blending (respecting HU statistics or MRI signal models) captures most of the augmentation benefit attributed to learned generative models for lesion segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: On low-prevalence lesion tasks, physics-aware pasting will recover a large fraction of the gap between no-augmentation and generative-augmentation baselines at a small fraction of the pipeline complexity.
why_important: If simple pasting suffices, small clinical teams can boost rare-lesion performance without training or validating generative models, which also eases regulatory review.
why_possibly_novel: Copy-paste augmentation is known; a systematic comparison against generative synthesis specifically for rare medical lesion classes, with modality-aware blending as the differentiator, appears not settled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a lesion dataset subsampled to simulate rarity, compare no augmentation, naive pasting, physics-aware pasting, and an available generative-augmentation pipeline, holding training budget constant.
main_risk: Pasted lesions may lack the anatomical context correlations (location priors, surrounding tissue reaction) that make real lesions detectable, capping the achievable benefit.
community_default_belief: Learned generative models are the state-of-the-art path to synthesizing training data for rare classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation networks mostly need local contrast and boundary diversity, which pasting supplies directly, while generative realism beyond that may be wasted effort.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One training run with physics-aware pasting on a subsampled lesion task; if it fails to improve over no augmentation at all, the premise collapses quickly.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Cross-modality label transfer fails mainly at boundaries, not textures: a boundary-band-weighted loss fixes most of CT-to-MRI label transfer.
problem: Labels are abundant for CT but scarce for MRI of the same anatomy; synthesis-based label transfer underperforms and the failure mode is poorly characterized.
core_hypothesis: After image synthesis or registration-based transfer, residual error concentrates in a thin boundary band where modality-specific tissue contrast disagrees, so boundary-band-aware losses and label softening recover most of the lost accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Error decomposition of transferred labels will show a large majority of disagreement within a few millimeters of organ boundaries, and boundary-band-weighted training will close a substantial share of the transfer gap without any new MRI labels.
why_important: A reliable CT-to-MRI transfer recipe would unlock MRI segmentation for anatomies where only CT labels exist, a common situation in radiotherapy workflows.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-modality synthesis for segmentation is well studied; the specific decomposition claim (boundary band dominates) and the corresponding cheap fix appear not to be standard results.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On paired or registered CT-MRI data with labels on both, transfer CT labels to MRI, spatially decompose the disagreement into boundary band vs interior, then train with band-weighted loss and measure gap closure.
main_risk: For some structures the modality disagreement is not a thin band but genuine topological difference in what is visible, which no reweighting can fix.
community_default_belief: The CT-to-MRI gap is a global appearance-distribution problem best solved with better image translation networks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Translation already matches global appearance well; what it cannot know is where the true boundary sits under different tissue contrast, which is inherently a boundary-local issue.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the boundary-band error decomposition on one paired dataset in a day; if interior errors dominate, the hypothesis is dead before any training.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Use unlabeled longitudinal repeat scans of the same patient as free consistency supervision for segmentation.
problem: Hospitals hold many repeat scans per patient that are ignored during training because none are labeled, wasting a uniquely structured form of unlabeled data.
core_hypothesis: Enforcing registration-mediated consistency of predicted masks across a patient's repeat scans is a stronger regularizer than generic unlabeled-data consistency, because anatomy is nearly constant while acquisition varies.
falsifiable_prediction: Semi-supervised training with cross-timepoint consistency on repeat scans will beat standard augmentation-consistency semi-supervision at equal unlabeled data volume, especially on cross-scanner test sets.
why_important: Longitudinal archives are ubiquitous and completely free; a training recipe that exploits their structure would improve label efficiency without any new annotation.
why_possibly_novel: Semi-supervised segmentation via augmentation consistency is standard; using real repeat acquisitions of the same anatomy as the consistency pair, with registration handling anatomical change, appears less exploited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble unlabeled repeat-scan pairs, add cross-timepoint consistency loss to a semi-supervised baseline trained on a small labeled set, and compare against the same baseline using standard augmentation-based consistency.
main_risk: True anatomical change between timepoints (disease progression, weight change) can turn the consistency signal into a harmful bias exactly for oncology cases.
community_default_belief: Unlabeled scans are interchangeable, and simulated augmentations are an adequate proxy for real acquisition variation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Simulated augmentations underrepresent real scanner, protocol, and positioning variation, whereas repeat scans capture the true nuisance distribution with anatomy held fixed.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Small-scale run on repeat scans from a public longitudinal collection: if cross-timepoint consistency does not beat augmentation consistency even on in-domain test data, drop the idea.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Reconstruction-kernel robustness for CT segmentation via learned frequency-response matching instead of image-space augmentation.
problem: CT reconstruction kernels (sharp vs smooth) shift image frequency content and measurably degrade segmentation models trained on one kernel and deployed on another.
core_hypothesis: Kernel shift is essentially a linear frequency-response change, so a small learned filter bank that matches the modulation-transfer characteristics between kernels normalizes inputs better than generic blur or sharpen augmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: A frequency-matching front end fit on a handful of paired kernel reconstructions will recover most cross-kernel Dice loss, outperforming random blur or sharpness augmentation at equal training cost.
why_important: Kernel mismatch is one of the most common silent deployment shifts in CT, since sites reconstruct with different kernels for different clinical questions.
why_possibly_novel: Kernel harmonization is studied in radiomics; wiring an explicit learned frequency-response matcher into the segmentation input path and testing against augmentation baselines appears less common.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use a dataset with dual-kernel reconstructions of the same raw scans, train on one kernel, evaluate on the other with and without the matching front end, and compare against augmentation-trained baselines.
main_risk: Modern iterative and AI-based reconstructions are nonlinear, so a linear frequency-matching model may not capture cross-vendor differences beyond classic filtered back-projection kernels.
community_default_belief: Heavy intensity and blur augmentation during training is the practical answer to CT kernel variability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation covers a generic family of perturbations; the actual kernel transform is a specific, nearly deterministic operator, and modeling it directly should be more sample-efficient.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fit the frequency matcher on a few paired-kernel scan pairs and measure cross-kernel Dice recovery in a single evaluation pass with an existing pretrained segmenter.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Predict per-scan HU calibration offset as an auxiliary task to stabilize CT organ boundaries across scanners.
problem: Hounsfield unit calibration drifts across scanners, protocols, and time, subtly moving intensity thresholds that segmentation networks implicitly learn.
core_hypothesis: Making the network explicitly estimate a per-scan intensity offset and scale (anchored to reference tissues like air, fat, and blood) disentangles calibration from anatomy and improves cross-scanner boundary placement.
falsifiable_prediction: A model with an auxiliary calibration-estimation head will show smaller cross-site boundary displacement on low-contrast interfaces (liver-kidney, muscle-fat) than an identically trained baseline, with negligible in-site cost.
why_important: HU drift is pervasive and invisible in QA; a segmentation-internal compensation mechanism would reduce a class of silent cross-site errors.
why_possibly_novel: Histogram normalization is standard preprocessing; treating calibration as a learned, reference-tissue-anchored auxiliary prediction inside the segmentation network appears less examined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train baseline and calibration-head variants on multi-site CT, evaluate boundary displacement statistics per site on held-out sites, and correlate improvement with measured inter-site HU offsets in reference regions.
main_risk: If modern scanners are better calibrated than assumed, the effect size may be too small to detect over seed variance.
community_default_belief: CT intensities are absolute and comparable across scanners because HU is a calibrated scale, so no per-scan compensation is needed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reconstruction algorithms, beam hardening, patient habitus, and contrast timing all perturb effective HU values in soft tissue by amounts comparable to inter-organ contrast differences.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure reference-tissue HU distributions across sites in existing multi-site data; if inter-site offsets are negligible, the mechanism has nothing to compensate and the idea dies.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Projection-domain-faithful noise injection beats image-space Gaussian noise for low-dose CT segmentation robustness.
problem: Segmentation models trained on standard-dose CT degrade on low-dose scans, and the standard mitigation of adding Gaussian image noise poorly matches real low-dose noise structure.
core_hypothesis: Low-dose CT noise is spatially correlated and object-dependent because it originates in the projection domain, so augmentation that simulates dose reduction through a projection-noise model transfers to real low-dose scans far better than image-space noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Models augmented with projection-simulated dose reduction will lose substantially less Dice on genuine low-dose scans than Gaussian-noise-augmented models, with the difference largest in low-contrast soft tissue.
why_important: Dose-reduction pressure is universal in CT practice, and screening programs run at low dose by design, making this a high-prevalence deployment shift.
why_possibly_novel: Dose simulation is established in reconstruction research; systematic evidence about which noise-simulation fidelity level actually matters for downstream segmentation robustness appears thin.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using a dataset with paired standard and low-dose reconstructions, train with each augmentation flavor and evaluate on the real low-dose arm, ablating noise-model fidelity from Gaussian to correlated to projection-domain.
main_risk: Access to raw projections is rare; approximate projection simulation from images may itself be too inaccurate to show the fidelity gradient.
community_default_belief: Noise augmentation of any reasonable flavor gives the robustness needed; the exact noise model is a second-order detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation errors on low-dose scans concentrate where correlated noise streaks mimic or mask boundaries, a phenomenon white noise never reproduces.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate an existing standard-dose-trained model on paired low-dose scans and check whether its errors co-locate with correlated noise structure rather than being spatially uniform.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Condition segmentation networks on slice spacing as an input token instead of resampling everything to isotropic resolution.
problem: Clinical CT arrives at wildly different slice thicknesses, and the standard fix of resampling to a common spacing destroys information or fabricates it via interpolation.
core_hypothesis: A single network explicitly conditioned on physical voxel spacing can adapt its effective receptive field and outperform both resample-to-isotropic pipelines and spacing-specific models when deployed across heterogeneous spacings.
falsifiable_prediction: The spacing-conditioned model will beat the resampling baseline on native thick-slice data, with the largest gains on small structures that interpolation smears, while matching it on thin-slice data.
why_important: Thick-slice scans dominate routine clinical archives, yet most research models are developed on thin-slice research data, creating a systematic deployment mismatch.
why_possibly_novel: Spacing-aware architectures exist in parts of the literature, but a controlled comparison isolating conditioning-vs-resampling as the design decision, across a wide spacing range, appears not to be settled practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a multi-spacing training set by physically consistent downsampling of thin-slice volumes, train conditioned and resampling pipelines at equal compute, and evaluate on genuinely acquired thick-slice test data.
main_risk: Simulated thick slices may not reproduce true acquisition physics (partial volume from helical acquisition), weakening conclusions about real data.
community_default_belief: Resampling to a fixed target spacing, as popularized by strong self-configuring pipelines, is the robust default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Resampling bakes an irreversible information loss into preprocessing; conditioning lets the network decide how to use anisotropic information per structure.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate an isotropic-trained model on native thick-slice scans vs the same scans resampled, quantifying how much error is attributable to the resampling step itself.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: An auxiliary contrast-phase classifier gates segmentation features to prevent failures on unusual contrast timing in CT.
problem: Organ and tumor appearance in contrast-enhanced CT depends strongly on injection timing, and models trained mostly on one phase fail unpredictably on off-phase or poorly timed scans.
core_hypothesis: Explicitly estimating the contrast phase and conditioning the decoder on it converts an out-of-distribution failure into an interpolation problem, improving robustness to intermediate and atypical phases.
falsifiable_prediction: Phase-conditioned models will degrade smoothly on held-out intermediate-phase scans, while unconditioned models will show abrupt failures, and the phase head's confidence will predict which scans are risky.
why_important: Contrast timing varies constantly in practice due to patient physiology and protocol deviations; robustness to it is a prerequisite for dependable deployment in oncology imaging.
why_possibly_novel: Phase classification is a known task; using the estimated phase as a conditioning signal for segmentation and evaluating on deliberately off-phase scans appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on multi-phase data with and without phase conditioning, evaluate on scans with atypical timing identified via aorta-enhancement measurement, and compare failure-rate curves.
main_risk: Phase may already be implicitly inferred by large models, making explicit conditioning redundant and the gains negligible.
community_default_belief: Training on a mixture of phases with heavy augmentation implicitly handles timing variation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mixture training averages over phases rather than resolving them, which can produce systematically hedged boundaries on structures whose enhancement flips contrast polarity across phases.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Probe an existing multi-phase-trained model with a linear phase classifier on its features; if phase is already linearly decodable and errors do not correlate with phase, conditioning is unlikely to help.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Physics-simulated metal artifacts transfer to real artifact robustness better than learned artifact synthesis for CT segmentation.
problem: Metal implants create streak artifacts that destroy segmentation quality near hips, spine, and dental regions, and real artifact-bearing labeled data is scarce.
core_hypothesis: Because metal artifacts follow well-understood beam-hardening and photon-starvation physics, physics-based simulation into artifact-free scans covers the real artifact distribution better than GAN-style learned corruption.
falsifiable_prediction: Models augmented with physics-simulated artifacts will retain more Dice on real implant-bearing scans than models augmented with learned artifact synthesis at matched augmentation budget.
why_important: Implant-bearing patients are common in exactly the populations (orthopedic, elderly, oncology) where automated segmentation is most used for planning.
why_possibly_novel: Both simulation and learned corruption exist; a head-to-head transfer comparison specifically for downstream segmentation robustness near implants appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert virtual metal into artifact-free scans via projection-domain simulation vs a learned corruption model, train segmenters with each, evaluate on real implant scans with expert labels near artifacts.
main_risk: Simulation fidelity depends on scanner-specific spectra and reconstruction details that may not be publicly available, limiting realism.
community_default_belief: Learned generative corruption adapts to real artifact appearance better than simplified physics simulation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: GANs trained on limited artifact examples mode-collapse to typical streak patterns, while physics simulation extrapolates correctly to unusual implant geometries.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Visual and feature-space distribution comparison between simulated and real artifacts plus a single fine-tune run on each; if physics simulation is grossly off-distribution, rethink before full study.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Learned mixing of multiple CT display windows as network input beats raw normalized HU for segmentation of low-contrast structures.
problem: Networks receive globally normalized HU values, whereas radiologists read CT through task-specific windows that maximize local contrast, suggesting an input-representation mismatch.
core_hypothesis: Presenting several windowed versions of the scan (soft tissue, lung, bone) with a learned per-pixel mixing layer recovers contrast that global normalization compresses, improving low-contrast boundary accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Multi-window input models will beat single-normalization baselines on structures whose boundaries span narrow HU ranges, and the learned mixing weights will concentrate on the clinically standard window for each structure.
why_important: It is a nearly free architectural change addressing a plausible systematic disadvantage of standard preprocessing across all CT segmentation tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Windowing as augmentation or fixed multi-channel input has been tried in places; the learned spatially adaptive mixing formulation with structure-wise analysis of what the network chooses appears less studied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Ablate input representations (single normalization, fixed multi-window channels, learned mixing) on identical backbones across two organ tasks and one lesion task, comparing boundary metrics.
main_risk: First-layer convolutions may already learn equivalent nonlinear intensity remappings, making the explicit representation redundant.
community_default_belief: A single clipped-and-normalized HU input is sufficient because networks can learn any needed intensity transform.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The first layer applies one shared transform to all inputs, but optimal windowing is structure- and location-dependent, which a spatially adaptive mixer can express and a global normalization cannot.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train small models with single-window vs fixed three-window inputs on one dataset; if there is no gap even at small capacity, learned mixing has no headroom.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Field-of-view truncation is a distinct, fixable CT failure mode: truncation-aware augmentation plus a boundary-of-scan flag eliminates most edge-of-FOV errors.
problem: Clinical scans frequently truncate anatomy (arms out of FOV, cropped abdomens), and segmentation models trained on complete volumes behave unpredictably near cut boundaries.
core_hypothesis: Models conflate scan-edge intensity discontinuities with anatomical boundaries; explicit truncation augmentation and an out-of-FOV indicator channel let them distinguish the two.
falsifiable_prediction: On truncated scans, truncation-trained models will show most of their remaining error away from the FOV edge, while baseline models will concentrate errors at the edge; in-distribution performance will be unchanged.
why_important: Truncation is mundane but ubiquitous in real archives and rare in curated research datasets, making it a classic silent deployment gap.
why_possibly_novel: Augmentation via cropping exists, but treating FOV truncation as a named failure mode with an indicator-channel mechanism and an edge-localized error analysis appears rarely done explicitly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create truncated variants of labeled volumes, quantify baseline error concentration near synthetic FOV edges, retrain with truncation augmentation plus indicator channel, and re-measure the spatial error profile on genuinely truncated clinical scans.
main_risk: The failure may be small in magnitude for modern models, making this an engineering note rather than a research finding.
community_default_belief: Random-crop augmentation already covers FOV truncation as a special case.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random crops during patch-based training never present the padded-reconstruction intensity signature of true FOV truncation, so the model never sees the actual artifact.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run an existing model on a few genuinely truncated scans and inspect whether errors cluster at the FOV boundary; absence of clustering kills the premise immediately.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Sequence-agnostic MRI segmentation through an intermediate quantitative-tissue-parameter representation instead of contrast-specific features.
problem: MRI segmentation models are brittle to pulse-sequence changes because network features entangle anatomy with acquisition-dependent contrast.
core_hypothesis: Forcing the network through a bottleneck that estimates pseudo-quantitative tissue parameters (proton density, T1-like, T2-like maps) yields a representation invariant to sequence choice, enabling one model to segment across arbitrary contrasts.
falsifiable_prediction: The parameter-bottleneck model will lose far less accuracy on held-out unseen sequences than a standard model trained on the same sequence mixture, and its bottleneck maps will correlate with true quantitative maps where available.
why_important: Sequence heterogeneity is the dominant obstacle to deploying one MRI model across hospitals, since protocols are never harmonized in practice.
why_possibly_novel: Synthetic-MR and sequence-augmentation approaches exist; an explicit physics-parameter bottleneck trained end-to-end for segmentation invariance, validated against measured quantitative maps, appears less established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on a set of sequences with the bottleneck constraint, test zero-shot on an excluded sequence type, and compare against sequence-augmentation baselines; validate bottleneck maps on any dataset with true quantitative imaging.
main_risk: The inverse problem from a single contrast to tissue parameters is underdetermined, so the bottleneck may learn a degenerate encoding that quietly reintroduces sequence dependence.
community_default_belief: Aggressive intensity augmentation and diverse training sequences are the practical route to sequence robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation covers interpolation between seen contrasts but not extrapolation to genuinely new sequence physics, which a parameter-space representation naturally supports.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Check zero-shot degradation of a strong augmentation-trained baseline on one truly unseen sequence; if degradation is already minor, the invariance problem is less severe than assumed and the bottleneck is unnecessary.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Treat MRI bias field as an explicit disentangled latent inside the segmentation network instead of a preprocessing correction step.
problem: Intensity inhomogeneity (bias field) varies with coil configuration and patient positioning, and the standard correct-then-segment pipeline propagates correction failures into segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Jointly inferring a smooth multiplicative bias latent and the segmentation lets errors in each inform the other, outperforming sequential correction, especially at high field strengths where bias is severe.
falsifiable_prediction: The joint model will beat the correct-then-segment pipeline on scans with strong inhomogeneity, and its inferred bias maps will be smoother and more accurate than the preprocessing tool's estimates where synthetic ground-truth bias is available.
why_important: Every MRI pipeline contains a bias-correction stage whose silent failures are a recurring source of segmentation errors, particularly in large-FOV body imaging.
why_possibly_novel: Joint bias-and-segmentation estimation has classical roots in EM-based methods; reviving it inside modern networks with a structured smooth latent and testing against the ubiquitous preprocessing default appears timely and under-done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply synthetic bias fields of controlled severity to clean labeled MRI, compare joint inference vs sequential pipelines across severity levels, then confirm on real high-field scans with expert labels.
main_risk: Modern networks may already be effectively invariant to smooth intensity modulation, leaving no measurable headroom.
community_default_belief: Bias correction is a solved preprocessing problem and segmentation networks are robust to residual inhomogeneity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Robustness claims are usually validated on brain MRI with mild bias; body and high-field imaging exhibit far stronger modulation where the correct-then-segment factorization demonstrably strains.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Apply strong synthetic bias to test scans and measure an existing model's degradation curve; if it is flat, networks are already invariant and the idea is unnecessary.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Spacing-conditioned 2.5D attention beats naive 3D convolution on thick-slice anisotropic clinical MRI.
problem: Clinical MRI is often acquired with thin in-plane resolution but thick slices, and isotropic 3D architectures handle this anisotropy poorly while pure 2D models discard through-plane context.
core_hypothesis: Processing slices with strong 2D encoders and exchanging information via inter-slice attention weighted by physical slice distance matches the data geometry and outperforms 3D convolutions whose kernels assume isotropy.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets with slice thickness several times the in-plane spacing, the spacing-aware 2.5D model will beat 3D convolutional baselines at matched parameters, with the advantage shrinking as data becomes isotropic.
why_important: Anisotropic acquisition is the norm in clinical MRI, so architecture choices tuned to isotropic research data systematically underperform where models are actually deployed.
why_possibly_novel: 2.5D architectures are common; making inter-slice interaction an explicit function of physical spacing and mapping the crossover point against anisotropy ratio appears not systematically characterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 2D, 2.5D spacing-aware, and 3D variants on the same anisotropic datasets spanning multiple thickness ratios, and chart performance against anisotropy to locate crossovers.
main_risk: Strong self-configuring 3D pipelines already adapt kernel shapes to anisotropy, potentially matching the proposed design and nullifying the contribution.
community_default_belief: Well-configured 3D networks are the universal answer for volumetric segmentation regardless of anisotropy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At extreme anisotropy the through-plane signal is closer to a short sequence of loosely registered 2D images than a volume, a regime attention handles more naturally than convolution.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Single comparison at one extreme anisotropy ratio between an adapted 3D baseline and the spacing-aware 2.5D model; no gap there means no paper.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Test-time feature-moment matching outperforms training-time augmentation for cross-vendor MRI segmentation at zero retraining cost.
problem: Cross-vendor MRI shifts degrade deployed models, and retraining or fine-tuning per vendor is operationally and regulatorily painful.
core_hypothesis: Most cross-vendor degradation in MRI segmentation is explained by low-order feature-statistic shifts that can be corrected at inference by matching feature moments to source statistics, without touching model weights.
falsifiable_prediction: Moment-matching at a small number of network layers will recover a large fraction of cross-vendor Dice loss on unseen-vendor data, approaching augmentation-heavy retraining while requiring only unlabeled target scans.
why_important: A weight-frozen adaptation method is uniquely compatible with medical-device regulation, where any weight change can trigger re-validation.
why_possibly_novel: Feature-statistic adaptation is known in domain adaptation broadly; establishing where it suffices specifically for regulated MRI segmentation deployment, and where it fails, appears practically unresolved.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-vendor labeled MRI, freeze a single-vendor model, apply moment matching using unlabeled target data, and compare recovery against fine-tuning and augmentation baselines per vendor pair.
main_risk: Some vendor differences (geometric distortion correction, parallel-imaging artifacts) are structural rather than statistical and will not respond to moment matching.
community_default_belief: Meaningful domain adaptation requires updating model weights or training with the target domain represented.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the perturbation is mostly a global intensity-and-texture shift, normalization statistics are exactly the right knob, and weight changes are overkill with regulatory downsides.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One-hour test: apply feature moment matching for one vendor pair using an existing model and unlabeled scans; if recovery is negligible, the low-order-shift assumption fails.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: K-space-based motion simulation is the right augmentation for motion-robust MRI segmentation, image-space blur is not.
problem: Patient motion produces structured MRI artifacts (ghosting, ringing) that degrade segmentation, but common augmentation approximates motion as image-space blur, which looks nothing like real motion artifacts.
core_hypothesis: Simulating motion by perturbing k-space lines during augmentation reproduces the true artifact family, and models trained with it will be robust to real motion cases where blur-augmented models fail.
falsifiable_prediction: On clinically motion-corrupted scans, k-space-augmented models will retain substantially more segmentation accuracy than blur-augmented models, and the gap will correlate with ghosting severity.
why_important: Motion is among the most frequent MRI quality problems, especially in pediatric, elderly, and acutely ill patients who are also the hardest to rescan.
why_possibly_novel: K-space motion simulation exists in reconstruction and quality-control literature; its systematic use and validation as a segmentation robustness augmentation appears underexploited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement k-space line-reordering motion simulation, train matched models with blur vs k-space augmentation, and evaluate on real motion-affected scans graded by radiographers.
main_risk: Real motion interacts with multi-coil reconstruction and partial Fourier acquisition in ways simple single-coil simulation misses, possibly capping transfer.
community_default_belief: Generic quality augmentations (blur, noise, ghosting approximations in image space) adequately cover motion.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Motion artifacts are coherent, structured, and anatomy-dependent; image-space approximations miss the periodic ghost replicas that actually confuse boundary prediction.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Inspect error maps of an existing model on a handful of real motion cases; if errors do not co-locate with ghosting artifacts, motion-specific augmentation will not help.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Predictable modality redundancy: which missing MRI sequence hurts multi-sequence segmentation is computable in advance from anatomy-contrast relationships.
problem: Multi-sequence segmentation models break when a sequence is missing at inference, and sites cannot predict whether their protocol subset will be sufficient before deploying.
core_hypothesis: The performance drop from dropping a sequence is governed by how much unique boundary contrast that sequence provides for the target structure, which can be estimated from unlabeled data via inter-sequence mutual-information-style measures.
falsifiable_prediction: A redundancy score computed on unlabeled multi-sequence data will rank sequences by their drop-induced Dice loss with high correlation, enabling sites to predict deployment feasibility without labels.
why_important: It converts an empirical trial-and-error deployment question into a computable pre-deployment audit, which is exactly what hospital IT and regulators want.
why_possibly_novel: Missing-modality robustness methods abound; a predictive theory of which modality is droppable for which structure, validated across datasets, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-sequence labeled datasets, measure actual Dice drops for every leave-one-sequence-out combination and correlate them against unlabeled-data redundancy scores computed independently.
main_risk: Redundancy may be model-dependent (different architectures exploit different cues), weakening any model-agnostic predictive score.
community_default_belief: Missing-modality performance must be measured empirically per model and dataset; there is no shortcut.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information content of sequences about a boundary is a property of the data, not the model, so data-side measures should predict the ceiling of any model's drop.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the redundancy score and actual drops for one dataset and one model; a weak correlation there ends the general claim quickly.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Joint denoising-and-segmentation training beats denoise-then-segment pipelines on low-SNR MRI because task-relevant detail is preserved selectively.
problem: Low-SNR acquisitions (fast protocols, high acceleration, low field) are increasingly common, and generic denoisers optimize appearance metrics that may erase exactly the faint boundaries segmentation needs.
core_hypothesis: A denoiser trained jointly with the segmentation objective learns to preserve boundary-discriminative detail at the expense of cosmetic smoothness, outperforming sequential pipelines built from independently optimized components.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched noise levels, joint training will yield higher boundary accuracy than sequential denoise-then-segment, and the joint denoiser's outputs will score worse on image-similarity metrics while scoring better downstream.
why_important: Low-field and accelerated MRI are expanding access to imaging globally, and their usefulness hinges on whether analysis survives the SNR cost.
why_possibly_novel: Task-driven restoration is an established concept in general vision; quantifying the cosmetic-vs-task tension specifically for low-SNR MRI segmentation, with the metric dissociation as the falsifiable signature, appears underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate SNR reduction on labeled MRI, train sequential and joint pipelines at matched capacity, and report the dissociation between image-quality metrics and segmentation metrics across noise levels.
main_risk: With enough training data the segmenter alone may become noise-robust, making any denoising stage, joint or not, unnecessary.
community_default_belief: Better denoising, as measured by standard image-quality metrics, produces better downstream analysis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Appearance-optimal denoising is a lossy projection onto smooth images; the information it discards is disproportionately low-contrast boundary evidence, which is invisible to cosmetic metrics but critical for segmentation.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Segment denoised vs raw noisy scans with one existing model; if raw-noisy segmentation already matches the denoised path, the pipeline question is moot at that noise level.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Implicit-coordinate decoders enable native-resolution MRI segmentation on arbitrary grids without resampling artifacts.
problem: MRI arrives on wildly varying grids, and resampling both inputs and outputs to fixed grids introduces interpolation error twice, once into the network and once into the clinical measurement.
core_hypothesis: Decoding segmentation as a continuous function of physical coordinates, queried at the native grid, removes output-resampling error and lets one model serve any acquisition geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: Coordinate-decoder models will match voxel-grid decoders in-distribution but beat them on out-of-distribution grid geometries, with the advantage concentrated in thin structures and volume-measurement accuracy.
why_important: Clinical measurements (volumes, diameters) are computed from masks, and resampling-induced measurement bias directly affects clinical decisions like treatment response calls.
why_possibly_novel: Implicit neural representations are actively researched; positioning them specifically as the fix for grid-heterogeneity in clinical MRI segmentation, with measurement-error endpoints rather than Dice, appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched voxel-decoder and coordinate-decoder models, evaluate across resampled and native test grids, and quantify volume-measurement bias against labels defined on native grids.
main_risk: Coordinate decoders can be slower at inference and may lose fine detail if the latent lacks capacity, negating practical benefit.
community_default_belief: Resampling to a canonical grid is harmless for practical purposes and simplifies everything.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For thin or low-volume structures the interpolation error is a meaningful fraction of the measurement itself, and it is systematically biased rather than random, which canonical-grid experiments never surface.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure the pure resampling round-trip error on existing labels across realistic grid pairs; if measurement bias is negligible, the motivation evaporates.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Speckle is signal: despeckling ultrasound before segmentation removes tissue-discriminative texture and hurts accuracy.
problem: Ultrasound pipelines often include despeckling as a cleanup step, assuming speckle is noise, though speckle statistics encode scatterer properties of tissue.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation networks exploit second-order speckle statistics as a tissue signature, so despeckling preprocessing strictly removes information and degrades boundary placement between texturally similar tissues.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained and tested on raw B-mode will outperform matched models on despeckled inputs, with the gap largest for boundaries defined by texture rather than edges, and texture-scrambling controls will localize the effect to speckle statistics.
why_important: It would overturn a common preprocessing default and redirect effort from despeckling toward speckle-statistics-aware architectures.
why_possibly_novel: The information content of speckle is known in ultrasound physics; a controlled demonstration that modern segmentation networks actually use it, and that despeckling is harmful, appears not to be common knowledge in the deep-learning segmentation community.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models on raw, despeckled, and texture-scrambled ultrasound across two organ tasks, and compare boundary accuracy with statistical tests over seeds.
main_risk: Effect may be dataset- and despeckling-algorithm-dependent, making the finding fragile or narrow.
community_default_belief: Speckle is multiplicative noise that obscures anatomy, and removing it helps downstream analysis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Speckle patterns are deterministic functions of sub-resolution scatterer arrangements, meaning they carry tissue-type information that convolutional features can decode.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one pretrained ultrasound segmentation model on despeckled test inputs; a significant accuracy drop already demonstrates the network relies on speckle content.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Estimate probe pose from image content and condition ultrasound segmentation on it to absorb operator variability.
problem: Ultrasound appearance depends on probe angle and pressure chosen by the operator, and this hidden variable makes cross-operator generalization notoriously poor.
core_hypothesis: A network head that estimates coarse acquisition geometry (insonation angle, depth setting, compression) from the image, used to condition segmentation features, converts operator variation from a nuisance into an observed covariate.
falsifiable_prediction: Pose-conditioned models will show a smaller cross-operator performance spread than baselines on multi-operator datasets, and ablating the conditioning will restore the spread.
why_important: Operator dependence is the central obstacle to scaling ultrasound AI beyond single-center studies, especially for less-experienced users in point-of-care settings.
why_possibly_novel: Operator variability is widely lamented; treating latent acquisition geometry as an explicitly estimated conditioning variable inside segmentation, rather than augmenting it away, appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset with multiple operators scanning overlapping subjects, train baseline and pose-conditioned models, and compare per-operator performance variance and worst-operator accuracy.
main_risk: Coarse pose may be unlearnable from single frames without external tracking ground truth, undermining the conditioning signal.
community_default_belief: Heavy augmentation and larger multi-operator datasets are the way to handle operator variability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation cannot simulate the physics of angle-dependent specular reflection and compression-induced deformation, but conditioning on estimates of them can explain the variation away.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train a probe-angle regressor on any dataset with recorded probe tracking; if angle is not decodable from images to useful accuracy, conditioning has no input signal.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Temporal cycle-consistency across ultrasound video frames as self-supervision that beats frame-independent training at equal label budget.
problem: Ultrasound is intrinsically a video modality, yet most segmentation training treats frames independently and labels only sparse keyframes, discarding temporal structure.
core_hypothesis: Requiring predicted masks to be consistent under forward-backward tracking between neighboring frames supplies dense self-supervision that regularizes boundaries and reduces flicker, improving accuracy per labeled frame.
falsifiable_prediction: With a fixed number of labeled keyframes, adding temporal cycle-consistency will improve both per-frame Dice and temporal stability metrics over frame-independent training, with the largest gains at the lowest label densities.
why_important: Label-efficient video training directly reduces the annotation cost of ultrasound AI, and temporal stability is itself a clinical usability requirement for live guidance.
why_possibly_novel: Cycle-consistency self-supervision is established in natural video; its quantitative value for clinical ultrasound segmentation under realistic label budgets, including probe-motion-induced appearance change, appears not well mapped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On an ultrasound video dataset with dense labels, subsample keyframe labels at several densities, train with and without temporal consistency, and chart accuracy and flicker against label density.
main_risk: Out-of-plane probe motion breaks frame-to-frame correspondence in ways optical-flow-style tracking cannot represent, potentially poisoning the consistency signal.
community_default_belief: Frame-level models with good augmentation are sufficient, and temporal modeling adds complexity for marginal gain.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The consistency signal is exactly complementary to sparse labels: labels give absolute anchors while temporal structure interpolates between them, a combination augmentation cannot replicate.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One run at the sparsest label density with and without the consistency loss; no improvement there, where the mechanism should be strongest, kills the idea.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Explicit acoustic-shadow map prediction as an auxiliary task makes ultrasound segmentation honest about invisible regions.
problem: Acoustic shadows hide anatomy below strong reflectors, and networks silently hallucinate boundaries inside shadowed regions where no evidence exists.
core_hypothesis: Jointly predicting a shadow-confidence map and conditioning the segmentation on it teaches the network to distinguish evidence-based from prior-based predictions, reducing hallucinated boundaries and improving uncertainty quality inside shadows.
falsifiable_prediction: Shadow-aware models will show better-calibrated uncertainty and lower confident-error rates inside shadowed regions than baselines, at unchanged accuracy in visible regions.
why_important: Confidently wrong boundaries inside shadows are a patient-safety hazard for ultrasound-guided interventions, where clinicians rely on displayed contours.
why_possibly_novel: Shadow detection exists as a standalone task; closing the loop by using predicted shadows to gate segmentation confidence and evaluating hallucination rates appears rarely done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate or simulate shadow masks on labeled ultrasound, train joint vs baseline models, and compare confident-error rates and calibration restricted to shadowed pixels.
main_risk: Ground-truth boundaries inside shadows are themselves guesses by annotators, muddying the evaluation of hallucination.
community_default_belief: Networks learn to handle shadows implicitly from data, and separate shadow modeling is unnecessary machinery.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training labels contain annotator-completed boundaries through shadows, actively teaching networks to hallucinate with confidence; only an explicit evidence signal can counteract that supervision bias.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure an existing model's confidence inside vs outside shadowed regions on a few annotated clips; if confidence already drops appropriately in shadows, the problem is smaller than assumed.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Physics-based ultrasound simulation from labeled CT anatomy as a zero-annotation pretraining source for ultrasound segmentation.
problem: Ultrasound annotation is scarce and hard to crowdsource, while CT archives with organ labels are comparatively abundant, suggesting a cross-modality bootstrapping route.
core_hypothesis: Ray-based ultrasound simulation through label-mapped CT volumes produces training pairs whose physics (attenuation, reflection, shadowing) is realistic enough that pretraining on them substantially reduces the real ultrasound labels needed.
falsifiable_prediction: Models pretrained on CT-simulated ultrasound will reach a given accuracy on real ultrasound with a fraction of the real labels needed by from-scratch training, and the benefit will persist after strong augmentation is applied to both.
why_important: It converts existing CT label investments into ultrasound capability, attacking the modality with the worst annotation economics.
why_possibly_novel: Ultrasound simulation for training exists in niches (guidance, registration); a systematic label-efficiency study for organ segmentation with modern simulators and strong baselines appears not settled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a simulation corpus from labeled abdominal CT, pretrain, fine-tune on varying amounts of real labeled ultrasound, and compare label-efficiency curves against ImageNet-style and self-supervised initializations.
main_risk: The sim-to-real gap in speckle statistics and probe-specific image processing may be large enough that pretraining transfers little beyond generic edge features.
community_default_belief: Simulated ultrasound is too unrealistic to be worth using; real data with augmentation is the only reliable path.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation transfer needs correct geometry-contrast relationships more than perceptual realism, and physics simulation gets geometry and shadowing exactly right by construction.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Pretrain briefly on a small simulated corpus and fine-tune on the smallest real subset; if there is no improvement over random or generic initialization even there, transfer is absent.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Simulate realistic time-gain-compensation curves as augmentation: gain robustness is a first-order factor for ultrasound segmentation, not a detail.
problem: Operators freely adjust gain and TGC sliders, producing depth-dependent intensity profiles that differ per exam, but training augmentation typically applies only global brightness-contrast jitter.
core_hypothesis: Depth-structured gain perturbations sampled from realistic TGC curve families cover the true intensity nuisance space of ultrasound, and models augmented this way generalize across devices and operators markedly better than globally jittered models.
falsifiable_prediction: TGC-curve augmentation will reduce cross-device and cross-operator Dice spread relative to global intensity jitter at matched augmentation strength, with gains concentrated in deep image regions where TGC effects dominate.
why_important: It is a cheap, immediately adoptable augmentation change targeting one of the most common sources of ultrasound appearance variation.
why_possibly_novel: Intensity augmentation is universal; parameterizing it by the actual physical control model of ultrasound devices (depth-dependent gain families) and demonstrating its specific value appears under-documented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with global jitter vs TGC-family augmentation, evaluate on held-out devices and operators, and analyze accuracy stratified by imaging depth.
main_risk: Public datasets often lack the device diversity to reveal the effect, requiring new multi-device data collection.
community_default_belief: Standard brightness and contrast jitter adequately covers intensity variation in ultrasound.
why_it_might_be_wrong: TGC variation is depth-structured, so global jitter never simulates it; the model's first encounter with a differently shaped gain profile is at deployment.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Apply synthetic TGC perturbations to test data and measure a jitter-trained model's degradation; if it is already invariant, the augmentation is redundant.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Segment freehand 3D ultrasound by uncertainty-weighted fusion of per-frame 2D segmentations rather than segmenting the compounded volume.
problem: Freehand 3D ultrasound compounds irregularly sampled 2D frames into a volume with spatially varying quality, and segmenting the compounded volume inherits all compounding artifacts.
core_hypothesis: Per-frame segmentation in original image space, fused into 3D with per-pixel confidence weights, preserves in-plane resolution and avoids compounding artifacts, beating volume-space segmentation especially where frame density is low.
falsifiable_prediction: Frame-space fusion will produce more accurate 3D surfaces than compounded-volume segmentation on the same sweeps, with the advantage growing as sweep irregularity increases.
why_important: Freehand 3D ultrasound is the affordable route to volumetric imaging in point-of-care and low-resource settings, and segmentation quality is its bottleneck.
why_possibly_novel: Both frame-wise and volume-wise processing exist in freehand ultrasound; a controlled comparison with uncertainty-weighted fusion as the differentiator and sweep irregularity as the analyzed variable appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On tracked freehand sweeps with 3D ground truth, run both pipelines with matched backbone capacity, and evaluate surface accuracy stratified by local frame density and angle diversity.
main_risk: Tracking errors corrupt frame poses, and fusion may be more sensitive to pose noise than volume-space methods that average it away.
community_default_belief: Compounding first, then applying standard 3D segmentation, is the natural pipeline since it reuses volumetric tooling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Compounding is a lossy, artifact-generating resampling step; deferring all spatial fusion until after inference retains information the volumetric pipeline destroys before the network ever sees it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For one sweep set, compare interpolation artifacts in compounded volumes against per-frame prediction quality; if compounding visibly destroys boundaries the network needs, the direction is promising.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: For cross-device ultrasound, per-device normalization-statistic adaptation with a handful of unlabeled clips beats adversarial feature alignment.
problem: Ultrasound models collapse across device vendors, and the go-to research answer of adversarial domain alignment is unstable, data-hungry, and hard to validate clinically.
core_hypothesis: Most cross-device shift in ultrasound is low-order (dynamic range, speckle grain, post-processing curves) and is absorbed by recalibrating normalization statistics with a small unlabeled sample, matching adversarial methods at a fraction of the complexity and risk.
falsifiable_prediction: Normalization-statistic adaptation using a small number of unlabeled clips per device will recover a comparable fraction of cross-device Dice loss to adversarial alignment across device pairs, with far lower variance across runs.
why_important: A minutes-long, label-free, weight-frozen commissioning step per device is deployable in clinics today, unlike adversarial retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Both techniques exist; the empirical claim that the simple method matches the complex one specifically for ultrasound device shift, and the characterization of when it fails, appears unresolved.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-device dataset, benchmark source-only, normalization adaptation, and adversarial alignment across all device pairs with several seeds, comparing means, variances, and failure cases.
main_risk: Some device differences involve geometric distortions and scan-conversion differences that statistics recalibration cannot address, potentially making results mixed and message muddy.
community_default_belief: Cross-device adaptation requires learning device-invariant features through adversarial or contrastive alignment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the shift is dominated by pointwise intensity processing applied by device firmware, matching feature statistics is the direct correction, and adversarial machinery is solving a harder problem than exists.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One device pair, one hour: recalibrate normalization statistics with unlabeled clips and measure recovery; negligible recovery falsifies the low-order-shift premise for that pair.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Stain normalization beats stain augmentation for pathology segmentation even if augmentation wins for classification, because boundaries depend on absolute color contrast.
problem: The community increasingly treats stain augmentation as strictly superior to stain normalization based largely on classification benchmarks, and extrapolates this to segmentation without direct evidence.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation boundaries between tissue compartments depend on absolute stain-channel contrasts that augmentation deliberately randomizes, so the augmentation-beats-normalization conclusion inverts for dense prediction tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched cross-scanner experiments, stain normalization will beat stain augmentation on boundary metrics for gland and tumor-bed segmentation, while the ordering reverses or disappears for patch classification on the same data.
why_important: Preprocessing defaults propagate through hundreds of pathology pipelines; a task-dependent inversion would correct a spreading overgeneralization.
why_possibly_novel: Stain handling comparisons exist mostly for classification; a task-stratified comparison isolating dense-prediction behavior appears not to be established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-scanner pathology data with segmentation and classification labels, run a factorial comparison of stain handling strategies across both tasks with matched budgets and multiple seeds.
main_risk: Modern strong augmentation pipelines may dominate both tasks, making the inversion undetectable and the result a null.
community_default_belief: Stain augmentation is the robust modern choice and normalization is a legacy preprocessing step.
