why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation teaches invariance to color, but segmentation needs sensitivity to color contrasts at compartment boundaries; invariance and sensitivity are directly opposed for dense tasks.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Single scanner-pair experiment on one gland segmentation dataset comparing the two strategies; if augmentation clearly wins on boundary metrics there, the hypothesis is dead.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: A low-resolution global-context stream beats larger tiles at equal compute for whole-slide segmentation of context-dependent structures.
problem: Gigapixel whole-slide images force tile-based processing, and structures like tumor beds and invasion fronts depend on context far beyond any affordable tile size.
core_hypothesis: For fixed compute, adding a heavily downsampled whole-slide context stream fused into tile features yields more accuracy than spending the same compute on larger high-resolution tiles, because relevant context is long-range but low-frequency.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched FLOPs, the dual-stream model will beat larger-tile baselines on context-dependent segmentation targets, while showing no advantage on locally decidable targets like nuclei.
why_important: It gives a principled compute-allocation rule for WSI pipelines, replacing the current ad hoc tile-size tuning.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-scale WSI models exist; the controlled equal-compute framing that isolates where global context pays off, with a locally-decidable control task, appears not cleanly established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep tile sizes vs dual-stream variants under equal-FLOP constraints on one context-dependent and one local task, charting accuracy against compute allocation.
main_risk: Fusion of misaligned resolutions may introduce engineering confounds that dominate the scientific signal.
community_default_belief: Bigger tiles at the highest affordable resolution are the way to capture more context.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Context signals (tissue architecture, region topology) survive extreme downsampling, so buying context via resolution is paying high-frequency prices for low-frequency information.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train one dual-stream model at a modest budget against the same-budget larger-tile baseline on a single context-dependent task; no gap means no story.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Point annotations plus a learned nuclear-shape prior recover near-full-mask performance for nuclei instance segmentation at a tenth of the labeling cost.
problem: Dense instance masks for nuclei are extremely tedious, limiting dataset scale, while nuclei have strongly regular shapes that should be exploitable as priors.
core_hypothesis: Because nuclear morphology occupies a low-dimensional shape family, a single point per nucleus combined with a shape-prior decoder constrains instance masks nearly as well as full outlines.
falsifiable_prediction: Point-supervised training with a shape prior will reach a large fraction of full-mask instance-segmentation performance, and the residual gap will concentrate in atypical nuclei (mitotic figures, tumor giant cells) where the prior fails.
why_important: Nuclei segmentation underlies quantitative pathology broadly; an order-of-magnitude labeling-cost reduction would directly scale dataset construction.
why_possibly_novel: Point-supervised nuclei segmentation exists; framing and validating the shape-prior mechanism as the reason it can approach full supervision, with failure analysis on atypical morphology, appears incomplete in the literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a fully annotated nuclei dataset, degrade labels to points, train with and without the shape-prior decoder, and stratify evaluation by nuclear morphology class.
main_risk: The clinically most important nuclei are precisely the atypical ones where the prior is wrong, potentially making the method unusable for its main application.
community_default_belief: Instance segmentation quality is bounded by annotation density; points alone cannot recover accurate boundaries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundaries of regular shapes are nearly determined by center location plus a low-dimensional shape code, so most of the outline information in full masks is redundant with the prior.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fit a shape model on existing masks, then reconstruct masks from centers plus per-nucleus shape codes; if reconstruction accuracy is already low, points plus prior cannot suffice.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Cross-scanner pathology shift is mostly a two-parameter problem: color transform plus blur kernel estimated at test time recovers most segmentation loss.
problem: Whole-slide scanners differ in color response and optical sharpness, degrading segmentation models across scanners, and current fixes involve retraining or heavy augmentation.
core_hypothesis: The dominant cross-scanner nuisance factorizes into a global color matrix and a point-spread-function difference, both estimable from unlabeled target slides, enabling a cheap test-time correction that recovers most of the performance gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Estimating and inverting these two factors per target scanner will recover a large majority of cross-scanner Dice loss across scanner pairs, and residual failures will localize to slides with focus artifacts rather than color issues.
why_important: A parametric, auditable two-factor correction is far easier to validate and regulate than retrained weights, fitting clinical deployment constraints.
why_possibly_novel: Color normalization is standard; jointly treating sharpness as a first-class estimated factor and quantifying the sufficiency of the two-factor model for segmentation appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On slides scanned by multiple devices, fit the two-factor correction from unlabeled data, evaluate segmentation recovery per pair, and ablate each factor to attribute the recovery.
main_risk: Scanner differences may include spatially varying focus and stain-dependent nonlinearities that break the global two-parameter assumption.
community_default_belief: Scanner robustness requires learning-based domain adaptation or training-time diversity; simple parametric corrections are insufficient.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scanner optics and color pipelines are engineered, near-deterministic systems, so their differences are naturally low-dimensional and parametric, unlike biological variability.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For one scanner pair, fit color-only and color-plus-blur corrections in an afternoon and measure segmentation recovery; if recovery is small, the factorization premise fails.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Artifact-simulation augmentation closes the frozen-section vs FFPE domain gap for intraoperative pathology segmentation.
problem: Models trained on high-quality FFPE slides fail on intraoperative frozen sections, which exhibit ice crystals, folds, and staining irregularities, exactly where fast automated analysis would matter most.
core_hypothesis: The frozen-section gap is dominated by a describable set of physical artifacts that can be procedurally simulated onto FFPE training data, transferring robustness without any frozen-section labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained on FFPE with procedural frozen-artifact augmentation will recover a large share of the performance drop on real frozen sections, with per-artifact ablations attributing the recovery to specific artifact simulators.
why_important: Intraoperative margin assessment is time-critical and understaffed; robust automated segmentation on frozen sections would have direct surgical impact.
why_possibly_novel: Domain gaps in pathology are heavily studied for scanners and stains; the frozen-vs-FFPE gap approached through procedural artifact simulation appears comparatively untouched.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build simulators for ice-crystal texture, tissue folds, and staining variation, train augmented and baseline models on FFPE, and evaluate on labeled frozen sections from the same tissue types.
main_risk: Frozen sections may differ in tissue morphology itself (cell swelling, freezing distortion), a biological difference no image-level augmentation can simulate.
community_default_belief: The frozen-section gap requires collecting and annotating frozen-section data; simulation is unlikely to capture its degradations.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most frozen-section degradations are physics-driven optical and mechanical artifacts with characteristic appearance, which procedural simulation reproduces well in other domains.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Simulate the single most prominent artifact (ice crystals), fine-tune briefly, and test on a handful of frozen sections; zero transfer suggests the gap is not artifact-dominated.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Deployment-compression-matched training matters more than model capacity for segmentation on compressed whole-slide images.
problem: WSIs are stored and transmitted with lossy compression whose level varies across archives, and segmentation models are typically trained at a different compression level than they encounter in deployment.
core_hypothesis: Compression artifacts perturb exactly the high-frequency content that boundary prediction relies on, so matching training compression to deployment compression yields larger gains than increasing model size, and boundary metrics suffer disproportionately relative to region metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: A small model trained at deployment compression will beat a much larger model trained at mismatched compression on boundary F1, and the mismatch penalty will grow monotonically with compression-level distance.
why_important: Compression settings are an invisible, controllable deployment variable; a quantified rule would be immediately actionable for every pathology archive.
why_possibly_novel: Compression robustness is studied in natural images; a systematic compression-mismatch study for pathology segmentation with the capacity-vs-matching tradeoff quantified appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-encode a labeled WSI dataset at several compression levels, train a model-size-by-compression grid, and evaluate all combinations on all levels, reporting boundary and region metrics separately.
main_risk: Modern architectures may be sufficiently compression-invariant that the mismatch penalty is trivially small, producing a null.
community_default_belief: Reasonable compression is visually lossless and therefore analytically harmless; model quality is what matters.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visually lossless is defined by human perception of texture, but boundary-precision tasks read exactly the quantization-damaged frequency bands humans ignore.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one trained model across re-encoded test sets at increasing compression; a flat curve falsifies the premise immediately.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Use restained or adjacent-section IHC slides registered to H&E as automatic pixel-level ground truth for H&E segmentation.
problem: Pixel-accurate tumor-region labels on H&E require expert time, while immunohistochemistry chemically highlights the same structures but on different slides or after restaining.
core_hypothesis: Registering IHC to H&E and thresholding the stain signal yields segmentation labels of near-expert quality at scale, and models trained on such labels match models trained on manual annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: H&E segmentation models trained on registration-transferred IHC-derived labels will match manually supervised models within noise on held-out expert-labeled test sets, with residual errors concentrated in registration-failure regions.
why_important: It industrializes ground-truth production for pathology segmentation, replacing expert drawing with routine laboratory staining plus computation.
why_possibly_novel: IHC-guided labeling has been used in isolated studies; establishing the recipe rigorously (registration quality control, stain thresholds, failure filtering) as a general label factory with quantified label quality appears incomplete.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On tissue with both restained IHC and independent expert H&E annotations, generate transferred labels, measure their agreement with experts, train on them, and compare downstream models against manually supervised twins.
main_risk: Section-to-section tissue differences and registration errors introduce spatially correlated label noise that may bias models in structured ways rather than averaging out.
community_default_belief: High-quality segmentation labels in pathology must come from expert annotation; chemically derived labels are too noisy at boundaries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: IHC reflects the actual molecular ground truth experts are trying to infer visually, so with good registration its boundary placement may exceed expert accuracy rather than fall short of it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Register a few IHC-H&E pairs and measure agreement between transferred labels and expert annotations; poor agreement at boundaries kills the label-factory premise early.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Attention maps from multiple-instance-learning WSI classifiers are poor segmentation labels for a predictable reason, and a gradient-attention hybrid fixes it.
problem: MIL classifiers trained on slide-level labels are routinely mined for attention maps that get used as free tumor-region annotations, without a clear account of when and why those maps are spatially wrong.
core_hypothesis: MIL attention identifies the most discriminative instances, not the full extent of the target region, so attention-derived masks systematically under-cover; combining attention with input-gradient evidence recovers extent because gradients respond to all class-relevant tissue.
falsifiable_prediction: Attention-derived pseudo-masks will show high precision but systematically low recall against true tumor regions, and the gradient-attention hybrid will substantially improve recall at comparable precision, improving downstream segmentation training.
why_important: Slide-level labels are nearly free while pixel labels are precious; making weak-label mining actually reliable would change data economics for pathology segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: MIL attention quality is often noted anecdotally; a mechanistic account of the under-coverage failure with a targeted fix and downstream validation appears not consolidated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train MIL classifiers on slides with hidden pixel labels, quantify precision-recall of attention maps vs gradient maps vs hybrids against those labels, then train segmenters on each pseudo-label flavor and compare.
main_risk: Gradient maps in large WSI models are notoriously noisy, and the hybrid may inherit noise rather than fixing coverage.
community_default_belief: MIL attention maps are a reasonable free approximation of tumor localization for downstream use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The MIL training objective is satisfied by finding a few decisive patches, so attention concentrating on discriminative subregions is an optimization consequence, not a bug that more training fixes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For one trained MIL model, compute the precision-recall of its attention mask against pixel labels on a handful of slides; if recall is already high, the under-coverage premise is wrong.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Promptable foundation segmenters lose to specialist 3D pipelines mainly because of slice-wise processing, not domain gap, and a thin cross-slice prompt-propagation module closes most of it.
problem: Promptable 2D foundation segmentation models underperform specialist volumetric pipelines on medical 3D structures, and the community attributes this mostly to the natural-to-medical domain gap.
core_hypothesis: The dominant deficit is architectural (no through-plane information flow), so adding a lightweight module that propagates prompts and mask context across slices recovers most of the gap without retraining the 2D backbone.
falsifiable_prediction: Attribution experiments will show larger error reduction from cross-slice propagation than from in-domain fine-tuning at matched budgets, and the combination will approach specialist pipelines on organ tasks.
why_important: It redirects adaptation effort from expensive medical re-pretraining toward cheap architectural add-ons, changing the cost calculus of using foundation segmenters clinically.
why_possibly_novel: Many medical adaptations of promptable segmenters exist; a controlled decomposition of the deficit into domain-gap vs dimensionality components appears not to have settled the attribution question.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On volumetric organ datasets, factorially combine in-domain fine-tuning and cross-slice propagation modules on a frozen 2D promptable backbone, and decompose error reductions per component.
main_risk: The two factors may interact so strongly that a clean attribution is impossible, muddying the headline claim.
community_default_belief: The medical domain gap is the primary reason natural-image foundation segmenters underperform, so in-domain training data is the answer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Slice-wise models discard through-plane continuity that specialist 3D models exploit as their main advantage; no amount of 2D in-domain data restores that information pathway.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare the same 2D foundation model's slice-wise vs naively-stacked-context performance on one organ task; if added through-plane context gives nothing, the dimensionality attribution fails.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Detector-generated box prompts plus a frozen foundation segmenter rival full fine-tuning for organs but fail for infiltrative lesions, with boundary ambiguity as the dividing line.
problem: Teams must choose between cheap prompt-based use of frozen foundation segmenters and expensive full fine-tuning, without a principled predictor of when the cheap path suffices.
core_hypothesis: Prompted frozen models perform well exactly when the target boundary is locally evident from image gradients, so a measurable boundary-evidence score dictates when fine-tuning is worth it.
falsifiable_prediction: Across structures, the gap between prompted-frozen and fine-tuned pipelines will correlate strongly with a boundary-ambiguity measure (local gradient strength along true boundaries), being negligible for crisp organs and large for infiltrative lesions.
why_important: It gives practitioners a data-driven decision rule for adaptation budgets, replacing folklore with a measurable criterion.
why_possibly_novel: Comparisons of prompting vs fine-tuning exist per-dataset; an explanatory variable that predicts the gap across structures appears not proposed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble tasks spanning crisp to infiltrative boundaries, run both pipelines, compute boundary-evidence scores from images and labels, and test the predicted correlation.
main_risk: Boundary ambiguity may correlate with other difficulty factors (size, contrast, label noise), confounding attribution.
community_default_belief: Fine-tuning on medical data is generally necessary for foundation segmenters to be competitive in medical imaging.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For high-evidence boundaries the frozen model's generic edge competence is already sufficient, and fine-tuning mostly teaches dataset-specific boundary conventions rather than new capabilities.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate the prompted-frozen pipeline on one crisp-boundary organ; if it already falls far short of fine-tuned performance there, the decision-rule framing collapses.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Foundation-model feature space as an annotation accelerant: propagate a few expert masks through a hospital's unlabeled archive via feature nearest-neighbor matching.
problem: Each new clinical segmentation project starts labeling from zero, ignoring that foundation-model features could identify unlabeled scans and regions nearly identical to already-labeled ones.
core_hypothesis: Anatomical regions with high feature similarity to labeled exemplars can inherit their labels with minor refinement, so archive-scale nearest-neighbor propagation multiplies effective label count early in a project.
falsifiable_prediction: Label propagation via foundation-feature matching will produce pseudo-labels whose quality on matched regions approaches manual labels, and training with them will beat training on exemplars alone by a wide margin in the first annotation rounds.
why_important: The first dozen labels are the most expensive phase of clinical AI projects; an archive-leverage mechanism compresses precisely that phase.
why_possibly_novel: Retrieval-augmented labeling is known in natural images; operationalizing it for volumetric medical archives with anatomical correspondence and measuring the cold-start economics appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate a cold start on a labeled archive by hiding all but a few exemplars, propagate labels via feature matching, quantify pseudo-label quality, and compare cold-start learning curves with and without propagation.
main_risk: Feature similarity may be dominated by acquisition style rather than anatomy, retrieving visually similar but anatomically inappropriate matches.
community_default_belief: Unlabeled archives are only useful through self-supervised pretraining; direct label transfer needs registration or extensive engineering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern foundation features already encode coarse anatomical correspondence, making cheap retrieval-based transfer viable where classical registration was too brittle.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Retrieve nearest neighbors for a handful of labeled slices in an unlabeled pool and visually audit anatomical correspondence; poor retrieval quality ends the idea within hours.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Medical segmentation pretraining scales with protocol-and-anatomy diversity, not raw volume count: a diversity-controlled scaling study.
problem: Groups assembling medical pretraining corpora optimize for total scan count, without evidence on whether marginal scans from already-covered distributions contribute anything.
core_hypothesis: Downstream segmentation transfer follows a saturating curve per acquisition-anatomy stratum, so corpus value is governed by strata coverage, and diversity-matched small corpora match much larger homogeneous ones.
falsifiable_prediction: Pretraining on a diversity-stratified subsample will match pretraining on the full corpus for downstream few-shot segmentation, while an equally sized homogeneous subsample will fall measurably behind.
why_important: Data acquisition and governance are the costliest parts of medical foundation-model efforts; a validated diversity-first rule would redirect collection strategy and budgets.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling studies exist for natural images and some medical classification; a controlled diversity-vs-count decomposition for medical segmentation pretraining appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From a large heterogeneous unlabeled corpus, construct subsamples factorially varying count and strata coverage, pretrain identically, and compare few-shot transfer across multiple downstream tasks.
main_risk: Defining and measuring strata (protocol, scanner, anatomy) is itself contentious, and results may hinge on the stratification scheme.
community_default_belief: More pretraining data is monotonically better; collection should maximize volume.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Within a homogeneous stratum, additional scans are nearly redundant given self-supervised objectives, so the marginal information per scan collapses long before corpus sizes currently pursued.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Pretrain on a small diverse vs small homogeneous corpus at equal count and compare few-shot transfer on one task; no diversity advantage there undercuts the thesis early.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Text-promptable medical segmentation fails on pathology-bearing regions when prompted with anatomical ontology terms but improves with radiology-report-style phrases.
problem: Text-promptable segmenters are being adapted to medicine using clean anatomical vocabularies, yet clinical targets are often pathological regions that clinicians describe in report language, not ontology terms.
core_hypothesis: The text embedding space aligns better with descriptive report phrases (which resemble pretraining text) than with formal ontology terms, so prompt phrasing is a first-order performance factor for pathological targets.
falsifiable_prediction: On lesion segmentation, report-style prompts will outperform ontology-term prompts by a measurable margin, while for normal anatomy the phrasing effect will be small.
why_important: Prompt vocabulary is a free design choice; knowing the right register could improve deployed text-promptable tools without touching weights.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-sensitivity studies exist for natural images; a systematic register comparison (ontology vs report language) for medical dense prediction appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched prompt pairs (ontology term vs report phrase) for a set of lesion and organ targets, evaluate a text-promptable model under both, and compare per-target deltas.
main_risk: Effects may be idiosyncratic to a particular model's text encoder, limiting generality of the finding.
community_default_belief: Standardized ontology vocabularies are the correct, safest way to prompt medical vision-language systems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Vision-language alignment is learned from natural co-occurrence text, where descriptive phrases dominate and formal ontology terms are rare, so ontology prompts sit in poorly calibrated regions of the embedding space.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Ten-prompt spot check per register on one lesion task with an existing model; near-identical results across registers ends the investigation cheaply.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Sequential site-specific fine-tuning of a shared medical segmentation model erodes rare-structure performance first; synthetic rehearsal of rare structures prevents it.
problem: Deployed medical models get fine-tuned per site over time, and nobody tracks which capabilities silently degrade during these serial adaptations.
core_hypothesis: Catastrophic interference is capability-heterogeneous: rare structures with thin training support degrade earliest under sequential fine-tuning, and rehearsal with synthesized rare-structure examples is sufficient protection without storing patient data.
falsifiable_prediction: Under simulated sequential site adaptations, per-structure degradation order will correlate inversely with original training support, and synthetic rehearsal will preserve rare-structure accuracy at negligible cost to adaptation quality.
why_important: Serial fine-tuning is the de facto lifecycle of clinical models; a privacy-compatible interference protection is an operational necessity nobody has standardized.
why_possibly_novel: Continual learning is a large field; the capability-stratified degradation claim and patient-data-free synthetic rehearsal in the medical segmentation lifecycle setting appear under-studied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate a chain of site fine-tunings across multi-site datasets, track per-structure metrics after each step, then repeat with synthetic-rehearsal buffers and compare degradation trajectories.
main_risk: Synthetic rehearsal quality may be the real bottleneck, turning the result into a statement about the generator rather than the interference mechanism.
community_default_belief: Light fine-tuning on new sites is safe, and any forgetting is roughly uniform and minor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Loss landscapes around rare-capability weights are supported by few examples, so even small gradient updates from new-site data can move them arbitrarily, producing targeted rather than uniform forgetting.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One fine-tuning step on one new site while tracking per-structure metrics; uniform degradation across structures immediately weakens the stratified-forgetting claim.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Distilling medical segmentation foundation models into deployable small models preserves in-domain accuracy but sheds out-of-distribution robustness disproportionately.
problem: Clinical hardware forces distillation of large segmentation models into small ones, and validation typically checks in-domain accuracy only, assuming robustness transfers alongside.
core_hypothesis: Robustness to acquisition shift resides in high-capacity redundant representations that distillation objectives do not target, so distilled students match teachers in-domain while losing a disproportionate share of cross-site robustness.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a distillation size sweep, in-domain Dice will degrade slowly while cross-site Dice degrades sharply below a capacity threshold, and robustness-targeted distillation losses will shift that threshold.
why_important: If validation-passing distilled models are systematically less robust, current deployment practice contains a hidden safety regression that standard testing cannot see.
why_possibly_novel: Distillation-robustness interactions are studied in classification; characterizing them for medical segmentation deployment, where the small model is the deployed artifact, appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Distill a strong multi-site teacher into students of varying capacity, evaluate all on in-domain and held-out-site test sets, and chart the divergence between the two degradation curves.
main_risk: The effect may be small for realistic student sizes, making it a theoretical concern rather than a practical one.
community_default_belief: A distilled model that matches teacher accuracy on the validation set is an adequate replacement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In-domain accuracy is determined by the decision boundary near the training distribution, while robustness depends on behavior far from it, which distillation on in-domain data never constrains.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Distill once at an aggressive compression ratio and compare teacher-vs-student on one held-out site; equal robustness there suggests the concern is overblown.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Measure interactive vs automatic segmentation in clinician-minutes: a click-budget benchmark that locates the crossover where promptable models beat automatics in real workflow cost.
problem: Interactive and automatic segmentation are compared on accuracy at fixed inputs, but the clinically relevant currency is total clinician time to an acceptable contour, which no standard benchmark measures.
core_hypothesis: When evaluated in time-to-acceptable-contour, interactive foundation models beat automatic pipelines on hard or rare cases but lose on routine cases, with a measurable crossover that should dictate hybrid deployment.
falsifiable_prediction: A time-based evaluation will reverse published accuracy-based rankings on a substantial fraction of structure-case combinations, and the crossover point will be predictable from automatic-model confidence.
why_important: Procurement and deployment decisions hinge on workflow cost, not Dice; the field currently cannot answer which paradigm saves clinician time.
why_possibly_novel: Click-count evaluations exist in interactive segmentation papers; anchoring evaluation in measured human time with acceptability thresholds set by clinical protocols appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument an annotation tool to record time-to-acceptable-contour for both paradigms across cases stratified by difficulty, with acceptability judged blind by a second expert.
main_risk: Human-time measurements are noisy and expensive, requiring careful study design to reach significance.
community_default_belief: Higher-Dice automatic models are better clinical tools, and interactivity is a fallback for failure cases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correction of a nearly-right automatic mask can cost more time than promptable segmentation from scratch when errors are diffuse, a cost structure invisible to Dice comparisons.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Pilot timing study with one clinician on a small case mix; if automatic-plus-editing dominates everywhere including hard cases, the crossover framing fails.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Structure-level failure prediction from cheap shape-and-size plausibility features beats voxelwise confidence aggregation for catching segmentation failures.
problem: Deployed segmentation needs a per-case failure alarm, and the default of aggregating voxel softmax confidences correlates poorly with the case-level failures clinicians care about.
core_hypothesis: Failures manifest as implausible global properties (volume z-scores, shape irregularity, topology violations, asymmetry) that a small classifier over such features detects more reliably than any function of voxel confidences.
falsifiable_prediction: On held-out failure cases, the plausibility-feature detector will achieve higher failure-detection AUROC than mean softmax, entropy, and confidence-percentile baselines, and will transfer across sites better than learned confidence heads.
why_important: A trustworthy per-case alarm is the single most requested safety feature for clinical segmentation deployment and a prerequisite for autonomous use.
why_possibly_novel: Quality-control-by-features has precedents; a rigorous head-to-head against confidence-based methods with cross-site transfer as the deciding criterion appears not settled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect model outputs across multiple sites, label case-level failures against ground truth, train the feature-based detector on one site, and compare detection metrics across held-out sites against confidence baselines.
main_risk: Plausibility features may miss failures that preserve shape statistics, such as a plausible-looking mask on the wrong structure.
community_default_belief: Better-calibrated voxel confidence, via ensembles or Bayesian approximations, is the path to failure detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Voxel confidence is local and self-referential (the model grading its own evidence), while shape plausibility is an external check against population anatomy that the model cannot inflate through overconfidence.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute volume z-scores and shape-irregularity features on existing model outputs and check their failure-detection AUROC against mean-confidence in an afternoon.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Calibration degrades predictably with shift magnitude: shift-conditioned recalibration keeps segmentation confidence trustworthy under scanner drift.
problem: Confidence calibration is fit on source-domain validation data, and under scanner or protocol shift the calibration silently degrades in the unsafe direction (overconfidence).
core_hypothesis: Calibration error grows as a smooth monotone function of a measurable input-shift statistic, so conditioning the calibration map on that statistic maintains calibration under shift without target labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Across graded synthetic and natural shifts, overconfidence will increase monotonically with the shift statistic, and shift-conditioned recalibration will roughly halve calibration error on shifted data relative to fixed temperature scaling.
why_important: Downstream clinical logic (review triggers, margins) consumes confidence values; unnoticed overconfidence under drift is a canonical silent failure of deployed systems.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration under shift is studied in classification; a quantitative shift-magnitude law and its use as a conditioning signal for dense medical prediction appear not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct graded shift series (noise, kernel, dose, vendor), measure calibration metrics per grade, fit the conditional recalibrator on synthetic grades, and test on natural shifts across sites.
main_risk: Different shift types may bend calibration in different directions, breaking any single scalar-conditioned model.
community_default_belief: One-time post hoc calibration on validation data is adequate, and shift primarily threatens accuracy rather than calibration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shift moves inputs off the training manifold where softmax scores are extrapolations; extrapolated scores are systematically miscalibrated even when accuracy degrades gracefully.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure calibration error of one model across a noise-graded test series; a flat curve falsifies the monotone-degradation premise immediately.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: A deterministic model plus registration-based anatomical anomaly checking matches deep ensembles for segmentation failure detection at a fraction of compute.
problem: Deep ensembles are the de facto standard for segmentation uncertainty but multiply inference cost by the ensemble size, which clinical hardware budgets often cannot absorb.
core_hypothesis: Most ensemble-detectable failures are also detectable by comparing a single model's output against a registered atlas-based expectation, because failures violate population anatomy more often than they violate inter-member consensus.
falsifiable_prediction: The atlas-check pipeline will match ensemble disagreement in failure-detection AUROC on cross-site test data while requiring one network inference plus one registration, and the two methods' missed failures will largely overlap.
why_important: If true, safety-relevant uncertainty becomes affordable on standard clinical hardware, removing a real adoption barrier.
why_possibly_novel: Both components are classical; the head-to-head claim that the cheap anatomical check matches ensembles for failure detection in deployment conditions appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-site data with known failures, compare failure-detection metrics and compute cost across ensembles, MC-dropout, single-model confidence, and the atlas-check pipeline.
main_risk: Atlas checks inherit registration fragility on pathological anatomy, potentially failing exactly on the abnormal cases where alarms matter most.
community_default_belief: Meaningful epistemic uncertainty requires multiple model evaluations; single-pass alternatives are second class.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ensemble members share training data and inductive biases, so their disagreement is a narrow probe; an external anatomical prior probes a complementary and arguably more clinically relevant failure axis.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run the atlas check on stored outputs of a model with documented failures and compare detection against stored ensemble disagreement on the same cases.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Learned aleatoric boundary-uncertainty maps can substitute for multi-rater data when estimating clinically acceptable contour tolerance.
problem: Defining acceptable contour tolerance for clinical QA requires expensive multi-rater studies per structure and protocol, so most deployments use arbitrary fixed tolerances.
core_hypothesis: A network trained with an aleatoric-uncertainty objective on single-rater data recovers boundary-uncertainty maps that approximate the inter-rater variability field, because rater disagreement concentrates where image evidence is genuinely ambiguous.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets that do have multi-rater annotations, single-rater aleatoric maps will correlate strongly with observed inter-rater disagreement along boundaries, and tolerance bands derived from them will approximate multi-rater-derived bands.
why_important: It would let every deployment derive structure-specific, image-specific QA tolerances without commissioning rater studies, improving both safety and practicality.
why_possibly_novel: The correlation between aleatoric uncertainty and rater disagreement has been noted qualitatively; validating it as a quantitative substitute for tolerance-setting appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train aleatoric models on one rater's labels from multi-rater datasets, compare predicted uncertainty fields against held-out raters' disagreement, and evaluate derived tolerances against multi-rater ground truth.
main_risk: Single-rater labels contain rater-specific systematic bias that aleatoric modeling will absorb as if it were image ambiguity.
community_default_belief: Inter-rater variability is a human factor that must be measured with human raters; model-internal uncertainty is not a substitute.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If raters disagree mainly where evidence is weak, the image itself contains the disagreement signal, and a well-trained ambiguity model reads it directly without needing multiple humans.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the boundary-wise correlation between aleatoric maps and rater disagreement on one public multi-rater dataset; weak correlation kills the substitution claim.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Test-time-augmentation disagreement is a stronger selective-prediction signal than learned confidence heads for routing segmentation cases to human review.
problem: Selective prediction (automatically deciding which cases go to human review) needs a reject score, and learned confidence heads are trained on in-domain data whose failure modes differ from deployment failures.
core_hypothesis: Disagreement under test-time augmentations probes model instability directly and generalizes to unseen failure types, whereas learned confidence heads overfit the failure distribution seen during training.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched review budgets, TTA-disagreement routing will retain higher accuracy on the automated fraction than learned-confidence routing, with the advantage growing on out-of-distribution sites.
why_important: Review routing directly determines the staffing economics and safety of semi-automated segmentation services now entering clinics.
why_possibly_novel: Both signals are known; the deployment-framed comparison under distribution shift with review-budget curves as the endpoint appears not established for medical segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-site data, compute both reject scores, sweep review budgets, and compare retained-accuracy curves in-domain and cross-site with statistical tests.
main_risk: TTA multiplies inference cost, which may itself violate the deployment constraints motivating the work.
community_default_belief: A learned confidence head, trained end-to-end, should dominate hand-crafted disagreement heuristics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned heads can only learn the failure statistics of their training distribution, while instability under perturbation is a mechanistic symptom that travels with the model to new distributions.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare the two reject scores on one cross-site evaluation with existing models; if the learned head wins out-of-domain, the central claim is falsified early.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Conformal prediction for segmentation should bound clinical scalars (volume, diameter) instead of pixel sets, yielding tighter and more usable guarantees.
problem: Conformal segmentation methods produce inner and outer mask bounds that are often too loose to act on, while clinicians actually consume scalar measurements derived from masks.
core_hypothesis: Calibrating conformal intervals directly on derived scalars exploits error cancellation over the mask and produces intervals tight enough for clinical decisions, unlike pixel-set bounds that must cover worst-case spatial errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Scalar-conformal intervals for organ volume and lesion diameter will be several times tighter (relative to clinical decision thresholds) than the same quantities extracted from conformal mask bounds, at equal coverage.
why_important: Distribution-free guarantees on the numbers clinicians actually use (for staging, response, dosing) are a concrete regulatory and safety asset.
why_possibly_novel: Conformal segmentation is nascent and pixel-centric; shifting the conformal target to derived clinical measurements appears largely unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both conformal schemes on organ and lesion tasks, verify empirical coverage, and compare interval widths against clinically meaningful thresholds across sites.
main_risk: Exchangeability assumptions break under site shift, threatening coverage validity exactly where guarantees are most needed.
community_default_belief: Conformal segmentation means spatial prediction sets; the mask is the object to be bounded.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Spatial bounds solve a harder problem than the clinical one; positive and negative boundary errors cancel in volume, so scalar intervals can be tight where set-valued bounds are hopeless.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On one dataset, compute the width ratio between scalar-conformal volume intervals and volume ranges implied by mask-bound methods; if similar, the tightness advantage vanishes.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Displaying boundary-confidence bands instead of binary contours measurably changes where clinicians edit and reduces missed model errors.
problem: Segmentation tools display crisp contours regardless of model certainty, giving clinicians no cue about which boundary segments deserve scrutiny during review.
core_hypothesis: Rendering calibrated confidence bands along contours redirects clinician attention to uncertain segments, increasing the detection rate of true model errors without increasing total review time.
falsifiable_prediction: In a controlled reader study, error-detection recall on uncertain boundary segments will be higher with band rendering than with crisp contours, with unchanged or reduced review time per case.
why_important: Human-AI review is the deployment mode of nearly all clinical segmentation; visualization is a cheap lever on its safety that is currently unstudied folklore.
why_possibly_novel: Uncertainty visualization is discussed in medical HCI generally; controlled evidence tying contour-band rendering to error-detection outcomes in segmentation review appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reader study where clinicians review model contours with and without confidence bands on cases with known seeded errors, measuring detection rates, edit locations, and time.
main_risk: Human studies are slow, need ethics approval, and effect sizes on small clinician cohorts may not reach significance.
community_default_belief: Clinicians want clean binary contours; uncertainty display adds clutter without changing behavior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention allocation follows visual salience, and reviewers currently distribute scrutiny by anatomical habit rather than by model risk, missing errors in unexpected locations that bands would flag.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Small pilot with a few readers and seeded errors comparing detection rates between renderings; a null pilot with reasonable power assumptions redirects the effort early.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Cross-orientation model disagreement (axial vs coronal vs sagittal models) detects protocol-shift OOD cases that reconstruction-based OOD detectors miss.
problem: OOD detectors based on reconstruction or density flag glaring anomalies but miss subtle protocol shifts that nonetheless break segmentation, leaving deployment unprotected against its most common threat.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on different orientations degrade differently under acquisition shift, so their mutual disagreement is a task-aligned OOD signal that fires exactly when segmentation reliability is compromised, rather than when images merely look unusual.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-orientation disagreement will predict actual segmentation error under protocol shift with higher correlation than reconstruction-error OOD scores, which will show near-zero correlation on subtle shifts.
why_important: Task-aligned OOD detection addresses the real deployment question, namely whether the output can be trusted, not whether the input is unusual.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-view consistency is used for semi-supervision; repurposing it as a deployment OOD monitor benchmarked against generative OOD detectors appears new in this setting.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train three orientation-specific models, construct graded protocol shifts, and compare correlation of each OOD score with true segmentation error across shift grades and sites.
main_risk: Triple inference cost and orientation models sharing blind spots on some shift types, muting disagreement where all three fail together.
community_default_belief: OOD detection is an input-modeling problem, best solved with density or reconstruction models independent of the downstream task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Input unusualness and output unreliability are weakly coupled; a scan can look typical yet break the model, and only task-space probes can see that.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On one shift type, compare disagreement-vs-error correlation against a reconstruction baseline using existing models; if the generative score wins, the premise falls.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Conditioning on a handful of DICOM acquisition fields recovers a large share of the multi-site generalization gap in medical segmentation.
problem: Cross-site degradation is treated as a high-dimensional distribution-shift problem, yet much of the shift is described by a few recorded acquisition parameters that models never see.
core_hypothesis: A small set of metadata fields (scanner model, kernel or sequence, slice thickness, dose or field strength) explains most site-to-site appearance variation, and conditioning the network on them converts unexplained shift into observed covariates.
falsifiable_prediction: Metadata-conditioned models will close a substantial fraction of the gap between single-site and multi-site-trained baselines on held-out sites, and ablations will identify a minimal sufficient field set.
why_important: Metadata is free and always present in DICOM; if it buys meaningful robustness, every clinical pipeline can adopt it with trivial engineering.
why_possibly_novel: Metadata is used for stratification and QA; systematic conditioning of segmentation networks on acquisition fields with gap-closure quantification appears surprisingly rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-site collections, train baseline vs metadata-conditioned models, evaluate on held-out sites, and run field-ablation studies to attribute the recovered performance.
main_risk: Metadata fields can be inconsistently populated or vendor-idiosyncratic, and conditioning may overfit to site identity rather than physical parameters.
community_default_belief: Robustness must be learned from pixel data via augmentation or adaptation; metadata is auxiliary bookkeeping.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The main nuisance factors in medical imaging are engineered acquisition choices that are literally recorded in the header, unlike natural images where nuisances are unobserved.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Regress per-case segmentation error of an existing model against DICOM fields across sites; weak explanatory power means conditioning has nothing to exploit.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Entropy-minimization test-time adaptation silently destroys small structures in segmentation; volume-preservation constraints make TTA safe.
problem: Test-time adaptation methods imported from classification are being applied to medical segmentation, where their failure modes on class-imbalanced dense outputs are uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Entropy minimization on dense predictions preferentially erodes low-confidence small structures toward the background class, so TTA improves average metrics while catastrophically failing on minority structures unless constrained by structure-volume priors.
falsifiable_prediction: Standard entropy-based TTA will improve mean Dice on shifted data while sharply increasing the rate of vanished small structures, and adding per-structure volume-preservation penalties will eliminate the vanishing at minor average cost.
why_important: TTA is attractive for clinical deployment because it needs no labels, but an unrecognized small-structure failure mode would be a patient-safety issue hiding behind improved averages.
why_possibly_novel: TTA failure modes are being documented in classification; the class-collapse mechanism specific to dense, extremely imbalanced medical segmentation with a targeted constraint fix appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply entropy-based TTA across shifted medical datasets, track per-structure metrics and structure-disappearance rates over adaptation steps, then repeat with volume-constrained variants.
main_risk: Results may vary strongly across TTA variants, inviting the criticism that only weak baselines exhibit the collapse.
community_default_belief: TTA that improves average segmentation metrics on shifted data is beneficial and deployment-ready.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averages are dominated by large structures; entropy descent has a systematic gradient toward majority classes that harms exactly the small structures clinical users care most about.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run one entropy-TTA method on one shifted dataset while logging small-structure Dice per step; no erosion trend falsifies the mechanism quickly.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Federated segmentation degrades boundary quality more than region detection under site heterogeneity, and per-site normalization layers recover most of it.
problem: Federated learning is the privacy-sanctioned way to train across hospitals, but how site heterogeneity distributes its damage across error types in segmentation is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Global federated averaging blurs site-specific intensity-boundary relationships, so boundary localization suffers disproportionately compared to structure detection, and keeping normalization parameters local restores boundary precision without sharing more data.
falsifiable_prediction: Federated models will show boundary-metric degradation exceeding region-metric degradation relative to centralized training, and per-site normalization will recover most boundary loss while leaving region metrics unchanged.
why_important: Federated training is often the only legally viable multi-site option, and knowing its error signature determines whether it is acceptable for boundary-critical uses like radiotherapy contouring.
why_possibly_novel: Personalized federated layers exist; the error-type decomposition claim for segmentation and its targeted validation appear not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train centralized, standard-federated, and per-site-normalization-federated models on multi-site data, and compare boundary vs region metric degradation patterns per site.
main_risk: Effect sizes depend heavily on the degree of site heterogeneity, and available multi-site datasets may be too homogeneous to show the signature.
community_default_belief: Federated averaging approaches centralized performance uniformly as rounds increase; degradation is a single scalar gap.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary placement depends on site-specific low-level statistics that averaging destroys by construction, while detection depends on shared high-level anatomy that averaging preserves.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare boundary and region metric gaps for one federated-vs-centralized pair on existing multi-site data; equal proportional gaps falsify the decomposition claim.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Aggressive intensity-style randomization can substitute for multi-site training data in CT but not in MRI, a modality asymmetry with practical consequences.
problem: Style-randomization augmentation is promoted as a universal remedy for single-site training, but modalities differ fundamentally in whether their site variation is intensity-like or structural.
core_hypothesis: CT site variation is dominated by intensity-and-texture transforms that randomization covers, while MRI variation includes contrast-mechanism and geometry changes outside the randomization family, so the single-site-plus-augmentation recipe succeeds in CT and fails in MRI.
falsifiable_prediction: Single-site CT models with heavy randomization will approach multi-site CT models on held-out sites, while equivalently augmented single-site MRI models will retain a large gap to multi-site MRI training.
why_important: Data-sharing costs dominate medical AI budgets; knowing when augmentation genuinely substitutes for multi-site data would rationalize collection strategy per modality.
why_possibly_novel: Style augmentation papers usually validate on one modality; the explicit cross-modality asymmetry claim with matched protocols appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Parallel single-site-vs-multi-site experiments in CT and MRI with identical augmentation families and budgets, comparing gap closure per modality.
main_risk: Augmentation family definitions can be gamed; critics may argue a better MRI-specific randomization would close the gap, making the claim about a moving target.
community_default_belief: Strong intensity augmentation is a modality-agnostic route to cross-site robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: MRI contrast depends on pulse-sequence physics that changes tissue relationships nonmonotonically, something no pointwise intensity transform family can express, while CT variation really is close to pointwise.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure gap closure from one strong augmentation recipe in one CT and one MRI cross-site pair; similar closure in both falsifies the asymmetry.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Segmentation networks secretly encode site identity and exploit site shortcuts; adversarially removing site-predictability improves worst-site performance.
problem: Multi-site training is assumed to produce site-agnostic models, but networks may internally route by inferred site and apply site-specific strategies that fail on unseen sites.
core_hypothesis: Site identity is linearly decodable from mid-level features of multi-site segmentation models, and this encoded shortcut inflates seen-site performance while depressing unseen-site transfer; adversarial site-invariance trades a little seen-site accuracy for better worst-case generalization.
falsifiable_prediction: Site-probing will reveal high decodability that correlates with per-site error patterns, and site-adversarial training will improve unseen-site Dice while slightly reducing seen-site Dice, shrinking the spread.
why_important: Worst-site behavior, not average behavior, determines whether a vendor can safely claim general applicability to regulators and buyers.
why_possibly_novel: Shortcut learning and domain-adversarial training are established; the specific measurement that multi-site medical segmentation models internally condition on site, tied to unseen-site harm, appears not demonstrated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train multi-site models, probe features for site decodability, correlate with error structure, then apply site-adversarial objectives and evaluate seen-vs-unseen-site tradeoffs.
main_risk: Site invariance may remove genuinely useful acquisition-conditioned processing, hurting everywhere and confusing the message.
community_default_belief: Training on many sites automatically yields site-agnostic representations; more sites is the whole answer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks exploit any predictive covariate, and site is highly predictive of appearance; nothing in the loss discourages internal site routing that fails off the training-site manifold.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Linear-probe site identity from features of an existing multi-site model; low decodability immediately deflates the shortcut narrative.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Adult-trained organ segmentation fails on pediatric scans in size-predictable ways, and anatomical scale normalization recovers most of the gap without pediatric labels.
problem: Pediatric imaging is chronically underrepresented in training data, and adult models are quietly applied to children with uncharacterized failure patterns.
core_hypothesis: The dominant adult-to-pediatric failure factor is anatomical scale and proportion rather than tissue appearance, so registering inputs to an age-normalized anatomical frame before inference recovers most performance without any pediatric annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: Adult-model error on pediatric scans will correlate strongly with patient size measures, and scale normalization will close a large fraction of the gap, with residual errors concentrated in genuinely age-specific structures.
why_important: Children are a protected, data-poor population where model failures have outsized consequence and labeled data will remain scarce for consent reasons.
why_possibly_novel: Pediatric domain gap is acknowledged; a quantitative decomposition into scale vs appearance factors with a label-free geometric fix appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate adult models across pediatric age bands, regress errors on body-size covariates, apply scale normalization, and re-evaluate to attribute the recovered fraction.
main_risk: Age-specific differences beyond scale (ossification, organ proportion, contrast dynamics) may dominate for the youngest patients, capping the fix where it is most needed.
community_default_belief: Pediatric performance requires collecting and labeling pediatric data; adult models are simply inapplicable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tissue-level appearance in children largely resembles adults while geometry differs systematically; geometry is fixable by computation whereas appearance would require data.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Correlate adult-model per-case Dice with patient size on one pediatric dataset; weak correlation kills the scale-dominance premise.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Organ segmentation robustness to unseen pathology: synthetic anatomy-deforming lesions as augmentation prepare models for disease they never saw.
problem: Organ models trained on mostly normal anatomy fail when large tumors, effusions, or post-surgical changes deform the anatomy, precisely when accurate segmentation matters clinically.
core_hypothesis: Robustness to pathological deformation is learnable from synthetically deformed and mass-inserted training volumes, because the required competence is geometric accommodation rather than pathology recognition.
falsifiable_prediction: Models augmented with procedural mass-effect deformations will retain substantially more organ accuracy on real pathology-bearing scans than standard-augmentation baselines, generalizing across pathology types not simulated.
why_important: The failure hits oncology and surgical-planning workflows, which are among the highest-value applications of organ segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: Lesion-insertion augmentation exists for lesion detection; using biomechanically plausible mass-effect deformation to robustify organ segmentation against unseen disease appears less developed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a mass-effect deformation simulator, train augmented and baseline models on normal-dominated data, and evaluate on curated real pathological cases spanning simulated and non-simulated pathology classes.
main_risk: Simulated deformations may miss the intensity-infiltration components of real disease, limiting transfer to purely geometric failure cases.
community_default_belief: Handling pathological anatomy requires training on labeled pathological cases of the relevant disease types.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The model's failure is often geometric surprise, not appearance surprise; geometry can be simulated exhaustively even though disease appearance cannot.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Test whether a briefly deformation-augmented model improves on a handful of real large-tumor cases; zero transfer means the geometric hypothesis is wrong.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Silent within-site model decay from protocol drift is detectable from label-free output statistics before any accuracy measurement is possible.
problem: Deployed segmentation models degrade as scanners are upgraded and protocols drift, but sites have no labels to measure decay and no trigger to know when revalidation is needed.
core_hypothesis: Distributional statistics of model outputs (structure-volume distributions, confidence profiles, shape features) drift measurably before clinically significant accuracy loss, providing a leading indicator computable from routine unlabeled operation.
falsifiable_prediction: In retrospective multi-year archives spanning scanner upgrades, output-statistic control charts will flag drift events with a lead time over accuracy-degradation onset, with a low false-alarm rate under stable periods.
why_important: Post-market surveillance of deployed medical AI is a regulatory requirement in search of a method; a label-free leading indicator is exactly the missing instrument.
why_possibly_novel: Data drift monitoring is generic MLOps; validating output-statistic charts against ground-truth accuracy decay on real clinical archives with documented protocol changes appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Replay a longitudinal archive through a frozen model, annotate sparse ground truth across eras, and test whether output-statistic alarms precede measured accuracy drops around documented protocol-change dates.
main_risk: True patient-mix changes (seasonal, demographic) may drive output statistics without any model degradation, generating false alarms that erode trust in the monitor.
community_default_belief: Model monitoring requires periodically labeled audit samples; unlabeled statistics cannot distinguish model decay from population change.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Protocol drift changes input statistics in ways that couple to output statistics through the model, while population change couples through anatomy; the two signatures are plausibly separable with the right feature set.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Check on one documented scanner-upgrade event whether output statistics of a frozen model shift detectably across the boundary; no shift means no signal to build on.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Rater-ID conditioning during training learns and corrects each annotator's systematic boundary bias, yielding a less biased consensus model than label averaging.
problem: Segmentation datasets mix annotators with systematic styles (consistent over- or under-contouring), and standard training absorbs a data-weighted average of these biases as if it were truth.
core_hypothesis: Annotator bias is low-dimensional and consistent, so conditioning on rater identity during training isolates per-rater offsets, and inference with a neutral rater embedding produces boundaries closer to unbiased consensus than any label-averaging scheme.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-rater data, rater-conditioned models queried at the neutral embedding will land closer to held-out consensus contours than models trained on pooled labels, and learned rater embeddings will cluster by measurable annotator style.
why_important: Systematic contour bias propagates directly into clinical measurements like tumor volume and margin definitions, so de-biasing the learned consensus has clinical significance.
why_possibly_novel: Rater modeling exists in classification crowdsourcing; the boundary-offset formulation for dense medical annotation with neutral-embedding inference appears not standard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train pooled vs rater-conditioned models on datasets with per-rater attribution, evaluate against held-out multi-rater consensus, and analyze embedding structure against known rater styles.
main_risk: Per-rater sample counts may be too small to separate rater style from case-mix confounds, since raters rarely annotate identical case sets.
community_default_belief: Averaging or majority-voting across annotators washes out individual bias adequately.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging removes bias only if biases are symmetric around truth, but contouring biases are often shared and directional (systematic over-inclusion of uncertain tissue), leaving residual bias in any pooled label.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure per-rater signed boundary offsets against consensus on one multi-rater dataset; if offsets are small or inconsistent within raters, there is no stable bias to learn.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Training on the full rater distribution as soft labels beats consensus-fused hard labels for boundary calibration and downstream clinical safety.
problem: Multi-rater annotations are conventionally fused into a single consensus mask before training, discarding the disagreement structure that encodes genuine boundary ambiguity.
core_hypothesis: Rater disagreement is signal about aleatoric boundary ambiguity, so models trained on rater-frequency soft labels will be better calibrated at boundaries and produce more clinically honest contours than consensus-trained models of identical architecture.
falsifiable_prediction: Soft-label-trained models will match consensus-trained Dice while showing substantially better boundary-zone calibration and closer agreement between predicted uncertainty bands and held-out rater spread.
why_important: Overconfident boundaries in ambiguous zones directly mislead margin-sensitive decisions in surgery and radiotherapy; honest boundary uncertainty is a safety property.
why_possibly_novel: Soft-label multi-rater training has been explored in places; establishing the calibration-and-safety advantage as the headline result with margin-relevant endpoints appears not consolidated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On public multi-rater datasets, train consensus vs distribution-supervised twins, compare boundary calibration against held-out raters, and evaluate a margin-expansion task consuming the uncertainty.
main_risk: With few raters per case, the empirical distribution is a noisy target and may teach spurious ambiguity patterns.
community_default_belief: Consensus fusion produces the best single ground truth, and training on it is the correct use of multi-rater data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fusion converts a distribution into a point estimate before learning, which is information destruction; the model can always be collapsed to a point estimate after learning, but not the reverse.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train both variants on one multi-rater dataset and compare boundary calibration curves; no calibration advantage for soft labels kills the core claim.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Label noise damages small-structure segmentation disproportionately, and size-stratified loss reweighting recovers the loss without hurting large structures.
problem: Label noise robustness in segmentation is studied on aggregate metrics, hiding how the same boundary-level noise magnitude translates into vastly different relative damage across structure sizes.
core_hypothesis: A fixed boundary-noise width corrupts a fraction of structure volume inversely proportional to structure size, so small structures suffer disproportionate gradient corruption, which size-aware loss reweighting or noise-width normalization corrects.
falsifiable_prediction: Under controlled synthetic label corruption of fixed boundary width, per-structure degradation will scale inversely with structure diameter, and size-stratified reweighting will flatten this curve at negligible cost to large structures.
why_important: Small structures (nerves, small vessels, adrenal glands) are often the clinically critical ones and are silently sacrificed by noise-agnostic training.
why_possibly_novel: Label-noise robustness methods abound; the geometric size-scaling analysis of noise damage and its targeted correction for medical segmentation appear not articulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Corrupt labels with controlled boundary-width noise on a multi-structure dataset, measure per-structure degradation curves, then apply size-stratified corrections and re-measure.
main_risk: Real annotation noise may not have size-independent width, weakening the transfer from synthetic corruption to genuine noisy datasets.
community_default_belief: Label noise is a uniform tax on performance that noise-robust losses address globally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The signal-to-noise ratio of supervision is geometric: the same 2-voxel boundary jitter is negligible for a liver and catastrophic for a nerve, so no global treatment can be optimal for both.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Apply fixed-width synthetic noise and compare degradation for the largest and smallest structures in one dataset; absence of the size effect refutes the geometric premise immediately.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: A learned guideline-embedding token lets one model train jointly on datasets with conflicting annotation conventions for the same anatomy.
problem: Public datasets define the same structure differently (with or without vessels, capsule, adjacent tissue), so naive joint training teaches contradictory supervision and per-dataset models waste shared anatomy signal.
core_hypothesis: Annotation conventions act like styles: conditioning the decoder on a per-dataset guideline embedding resolves the contradictions, letting shared encoders exploit all data while decoders express each convention on demand.
falsifiable_prediction: Guideline-conditioned joint training will beat both naive pooling and per-dataset training on every constituent dataset, and interpolating embeddings will produce anatomically coherent intermediate conventions.
why_important: It unlocks joint training over the fragmented landscape of public medical datasets, effectively multiplying usable supervision for every structure.
why_possibly_novel: Dataset-conditioning is used in multi-task settings; framing annotation-protocol conflict as the target problem with convention-interpolation as evidence appears fresh for medical segmentation.
