minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble datasets with documented convention conflicts for one organ, train pooled, per-dataset, and conditioned variants, and evaluate each on each dataset's own convention.
main_risk: Convention differences may be entangled with acquisition differences across datasets, letting the token absorb domain shift rather than annotation semantics.
community_default_belief: Datasets with incompatible label definitions cannot be merged and must be handled by separate models or relabeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The conflicting part of supervision is a thin boundary-region minority of voxels; a low-dimensional conditioning signal suffices to switch it while the shared majority trains the common representation.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two-dataset pilot with one known convention conflict; if conditioning fails to beat per-dataset models there, the mechanism does not work.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Automatic label-audit tool: cross-slice consistency between labels and model predictions localizes annotation errors in existing datasets.
problem: Established medical segmentation datasets contain slice-level annotation errors (skipped slices, orientation slips, wrong-structure labels) that nobody systematically audits, corrupting both training and evaluation.
core_hypothesis: Annotation errors break the smooth through-plane continuity that real anatomy obeys, so disagreement spikes between a trained model and labels that co-occur with continuity violations pinpoint label errors with high precision.
falsifiable_prediction: The audit score will rank truly mislabeled slices far above correctly labeled hard slices, verified by expert re-review of flagged samples, achieving high precision in the top-ranked fraction.
why_important: Label errors in test sets distort every published comparison on affected benchmarks; a cheap audit tool has field-wide corrective value.
why_possibly_novel: Label-error detection is active in classification; a continuity-plus-disagreement formulation specific to volumetric segmentation with expert-verified precision estimates appears not standard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the audit on a public dataset, have blinded experts adjudicate the top flagged slices against matched controls, and report the precision of flagged items.
main_risk: The tool may flag genuinely ambiguous pathology as errors, requiring careful adjudication protocols to interpret precision.
community_default_belief: Public benchmark labels are reliable enough that observed model errors reflect model deficiencies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotation was done slice-by-slice by humans under time pressure, a workflow that structurally produces continuity violations models do not make, giving a separable error signature.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the audit score on one dataset and manually inspect the top ten flagged slices; if most are model errors rather than label errors, precision is too low to matter.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Boundary-tolerance-aware training: ignore label errors within the inter-rater band and gain stability without losing clinically meaningful accuracy.
problem: Losses penalize every voxel disagreement equally, forcing models to fit the sub-rater-noise component of labels, which wastes capacity and destabilizes training on the least meaningful part of the signal.
core_hypothesis: Zeroing or down-weighting loss within a structure-specific tolerance band around labeled boundaries removes gradient noise without removing clinical signal, improving cross-dataset generalization and seed stability at unchanged clinically-relevant accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Band-tolerant training will reduce seed-to-seed variance and improve out-of-dataset transfer while leaving surface distances beyond the tolerance band unchanged, with band width matched to measured inter-rater variability.
why_important: Everyone trains against noisy boundaries; a principled tolerance mechanism benefits nearly every medical segmentation pipeline at zero data cost.
why_possibly_novel: Loss-weighting near boundaries exists in both directions (often up-weighting); grounding the ignored band in measured inter-rater tolerance and testing generalization consequences appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate inter-rater bands per structure from multi-rater data, train tolerant vs standard losses across seeds and datasets, and compare variance, transfer, and beyond-band accuracy.
main_risk: Boundary up-weighting is popular because boundaries carry signal; ignoring the band may forfeit the supervision that sharpens boundary features.
community_default_belief: Boundary voxels deserve extra loss weight because boundaries are what segmentation is about.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Within the rater-noise band the labels are effectively random, and up-weighting random targets amplifies noise; the informative boundary signal lives at the band edges, not inside it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train one model pair with and without the tolerance band on a dataset with known inter-rater bands; worse beyond-band accuracy for the tolerant model refutes the free-lunch claim.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Many trainee-quality labels plus a hierarchical noise model beat few expert labels at equal cost for training clinical segmentation models.
problem: Projects allocate scarce expert time to produce small gold-standard training sets, while abundant cheaper annotators (trainees, technologists) are excluded for quality concerns, without a quantitative cost-quality tradeoff.
core_hypothesis: Trainee errors are largely random around expert consensus while cost per label is several times lower, so at equal budget the trainee-heavy strategy provides more effective supervision when combined with a noise model that estimates per-annotator reliability.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched annotation cost, models trained on noise-modeled trainee labels will match or beat expert-only training, with the crossover budget identifiable, and the noise model's reliability estimates will correlate with annotators' measured skill.
why_important: It would change staffing strategy for every medical annotation campaign, converting the expert bottleneck into a scalable supervised pipeline with experts only in audit roles.
why_possibly_novel: Crowd-labeling theory is developed for classification; the cost-anchored comparison with dense-annotation noise modeling in medical segmentation appears not empirically settled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect parallel expert and trainee annotations on the same volumes with recorded times, train under matched-budget allocations with and without noise modeling, and compare against expert-consensus test labels.
main_risk: Trainee errors may be systematically biased on exactly the difficult cases (subtle boundaries, pathology), violating the random-error assumption where it matters.
community_default_belief: Medical ground truth requires expert annotators; non-expert labels introduce unacceptable clinical risk.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For many structures the task is visual boundary tracing rather than diagnostic judgment, and tracing skill saturates quickly with training, making the expert premium mostly unnecessary.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure trainee-vs-expert agreement structure on a small parallel-annotation pilot; strongly biased (non-random) trainee errors on hard cases undermine the premise before any training.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Self-training loops progressively over-smooth segmentation boundaries, and injected boundary-sharpness regularization halts the drift.
problem: Iterative pseudo-labeling is standard for exploiting unlabeled medical data, but its cumulative effect on boundary geometry over generations is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Each pseudo-label generation regresses boundaries toward smooth average shapes because the model's uncertain boundary predictions are consumed as confident targets, so curvature-rich anatomical detail erodes monotonically across iterations.
falsifiable_prediction: Boundary curvature statistics of pseudo-labels will decrease measurably per self-training generation while region metrics stay flat, and matching the curvature distribution to the labeled seed set will stop the erosion without hurting Dice.
why_important: Self-training is a workhorse of annotation-scarce medical AI, and a hidden geometric degradation mode would affect fine-detail structures across many deployed pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: Confirmation bias in self-training is known; identifying and quantifying boundary-geometry drift as its dense-prediction signature, with a distribution-matching fix, appears not documented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run multi-generation self-training on standard datasets while logging boundary-geometry statistics per generation, then add curvature-matching regularization and compare drift curves.
main_risk: The effect may saturate after one generation at negligible magnitude, making it real but unimportant.
community_default_belief: Self-training with confidence thresholds is safe, and errors mainly enter through wholesale wrong pseudo-labels rather than geometric drift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging is intrinsic to the student learning the teacher's uncertainty-weighted mean boundary; thresholds filter whole samples but cannot filter the within-boundary smoothing that happens on accepted samples.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two generations of self-training on one dataset with curvature logging; flat curvature curves falsify the drift mechanism cheaply.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: The detect-then-segment advantage for small lesions has a predictable size threshold derivable from resolution and architecture, below which one-stage segmentation cannot compete.
problem: Whether to use one-stage segmentation or detection-followed-by-segmentation for lesions is decided by trial and error per project, with no quantitative rule for when each wins.
core_hypothesis: One-stage segmentation fails on lesions whose diameter falls below a threshold set by effective receptive-field statistics and class imbalance, while detection objectives remain sensitive; the crossover diameter is predictable from architecture and voxel spacing.
falsifiable_prediction: Across lesion datasets binned by size, the one-stage-vs-two-stage recall gap will open below a diameter predictable from network downsampling structure, and interventions that shift the effective resolution will shift the crossover accordingly.
why_important: Small-lesion sensitivity drives screening and staging use cases; a predictive design rule would replace expensive per-project architecture searches.
why_possibly_novel: Two-stage superiority for small objects is folklore in places; an explanatory, quantitatively predictive account tied to architecture parameters appears missing for medical lesions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched one-stage and two-stage pipelines on multi-size lesion data, chart size-binned recall gaps, and test whether architectural resolution manipulations move the crossover as predicted.
main_risk: The crossover may be dominated by loss design and sampling strategy rather than architecture, making the predictive rule unstable.
community_default_belief: With proper loss weighting and sampling, one-stage segmentation handles small lesions adequately, and two-stage pipelines are legacy complexity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Voxel-level objectives dilute the gradient contribution of tiny lesions below what any reweighting can recover, while objectives with per-instance normalization structurally protect small-object learning.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Size-binned recall comparison of one existing one-stage and one two-stage model on the same lesion dataset; no size-dependent gap refutes the premise.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Dice-optimal lesion models are lesion-recall-suboptimal: quantify the voxel-overlap vs instance-detection frontier and give practitioners the trade-off dial.
problem: Lesion segmentation is trained and selected by voxel-overlap metrics, but clinical value often depends on not missing lesions, and the tension between these objectives is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Voxel-level objectives implicitly weight lesions by volume, sacrificing small-instance recall for large-instance overlap, so instance-aware losses trace an accessible frontier between mean Dice and lesion-level recall that model selection currently ignores.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping the instance-weighting coefficient will trace a smooth frontier where lesion recall rises as mean Dice mildly falls, and standard Dice-selected checkpoints will sit at an extreme, recall-poor end of that frontier.
why_important: Missed lesions are the costliest clinical error in oncology screening and follow-up, yet the standard training pipeline systematically optimizes away from finding them.
why_possibly_novel: Instance-aware losses exist; the explicit frontier characterization and the demonstration that common practice sits at its worst clinical corner appear not established as a general result.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multifocal lesion datasets, sweep instance-weighted losses at matched budgets, plot the Dice-vs-lesion-recall frontier, and locate standard baselines on it.
main_risk: The frontier may be nearly degenerate (recall gains negligible before Dice collapses), making the trade-off practically uninteresting.
community_default_belief: Optimizing and selecting by mean Dice yields models that are also clinically sensible for lesion finding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mean Dice is mathematically dominated by the largest lesions and says almost nothing about whether the tenth small metastasis was found at all.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one Dice-selected checkpoint for lesion-level recall stratified by size; strong small-lesion recall would immediately weaken the motivating tension.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Conditioning on the registered prior-timepoint mask makes longitudinal lesion measurements consistent enough to change response-assessment reliability, independent of per-scan accuracy.
problem: Tumor response assessment depends on measured change between timepoints, but models segment each scan independently, so measurement noise between visits swamps true change for slow-growing disease.
core_hypothesis: Feeding the registered previous mask as a conditioning input correlates the errors across timepoints, reducing change-measurement variance substantially even when single-timepoint accuracy is unchanged.
falsifiable_prediction: On repeat-scan pairs with stable disease, prior-conditioned models will show much lower measured-change variance than independent segmentation, while retaining sensitivity to true progression in confirmed-change cases.
why_important: Response decisions (continue, switch, or stop therapy) hinge on change estimates; variance reduction there is directly patient-relevant even with zero Dice improvement.
why_possibly_novel: Longitudinal segmentation exists; framing error-correlation-for-change-measurement as the objective, evaluated on test-retest variance rather than accuracy, appears uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use short-interval repeat scans (minimal true change) to measure change-noise for both pipelines, and confirmed progression cases to verify preserved sensitivity, reporting a variance-vs-sensitivity analysis.
main_risk: Prior conditioning may anchor the model against detecting true change, trading measurement noise for progression-detection latency, the clinically worse error.
community_default_belief: Better per-scan segmentation accuracy is the route to better longitudinal measurement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Change variance depends on error covariance between visits, not marginal error; two mediocre but correlated measurements beat two excellent independent ones for difference estimation.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Segment a set of short-interval repeat pairs both ways and compare measured-change distributions; if conditioning does not shrink the stable-case spread, the mechanism fails.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Infiltrative tumor margins should be modeled as occupancy-fraction fields, not binary masks; hard labels are the wrong model class for gliomas and similar tumors.
problem: Infiltrative tumors have no true binary boundary at imaging resolution, yet datasets and models force a hard contour, producing unstable labels and misleading margin definitions.
core_hypothesis: Representing tumor extent as a continuous occupancy field trained from multi-rater soft labels and signal intensities yields more reproducible and biologically faithful margins than binary segmentation with any loss.
falsifiable_prediction: Occupancy models will show markedly better test-retest reproducibility of derived isocontours across raters and scans than binary models, and their gradients will align with the known imaging appearance of infiltration better than binary boundaries.
why_important: Margin definitions drive radiotherapy target volumes and surgical planning for infiltrative tumors; a representation-level fix addresses a foundational mismatch rather than an incremental accuracy gap.
why_possibly_novel: Soft segmentation outputs exist; elevating occupancy to the label and evaluation representation for infiltrative tumors, with reproducibility as the primary endpoint, appears not standard.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-rater infiltrative tumor data, train binary and occupancy models, derive matched isocontours, and compare inter-rater and test-retest reproducibility of clinically used margin surfaces.
main_risk: Without histological ground truth, validating biological faithfulness is indirect, and reviewers may see only a recalibrated version of soft binary outputs.
community_default_belief: Binary masks with good uncertainty estimates are an adequate representation for all tumor types.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For infiltrative disease, the underlying truth is a spatial density of tumor cells, so binary labels inject irreducible quantization noise that no uncertainty layer on top can remove.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure inter-rater contour variance on an infiltrative vs a well-circumscribed tumor dataset; if variance is similar, the binary representation is not the bottleneck claimed.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Cross-slice instance memory eliminates the merge-split errors that corrupt lesion counting and per-lesion measurement in 3D pipelines.
problem: Multifocal disease requires per-lesion identity for counting and tracking, but slice-wise or patch-wise processing fragments lesions or merges neighbors, corrupting instance-level outputs even when voxel masks look fine.
core_hypothesis: Maintaining an explicit instance-memory state across slices, in the style of video object tracking, resolves identity assignment better than post hoc connected-component analysis on merged probability maps.
falsifiable_prediction: Memory-based instance handling will substantially reduce merge and split error rates on densely multifocal cases relative to connected-component baselines, with the advantage concentrated where lesions are near-adjacent.
why_important: Lesion counts and per-lesion diameters feed staging and response criteria directly; instance errors corrupt these numbers even when Dice is high.
why_possibly_novel: Tracking-style memory comes from video segmentation; its application to through-plane instance identity in volumetric multifocal disease with instance-error endpoints appears underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multifocal datasets with instance labels, compare merge-split error rates and count accuracy between memory-based and component-based pipelines, stratified by inter-lesion distance.
main_risk: The prevalence of near-adjacent lesion configurations may be low enough that aggregate clinical benefit is marginal despite mechanism-level wins.
community_default_belief: Connected components over a good semantic mask is a sufficient instance extractor for medical lesions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Semantic probability maps of adjacent lesions overlap by construction, so no thresholding can recover identity; identity must be carried through inference, not reconstructed afterwards.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Count merge-split errors of a strong semantic baseline on the most multifocal subset of one dataset; if error rates are already negligible, the problem does not need solving.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Peritumoral edema vs tumor-core confusions follow modality-predictable patterns, enabling sequence-aware gating to fix a known error class without new data.
problem: Models segmenting tumor subregions systematically confuse edema with core tissue, and these confusions are treated as generic errors rather than analyzed against the imaging physics that differentiates the compartments.
core_hypothesis: Each confusion type is driven by over-reliance on a specific sequence contrast where the compartments look alike, so a gating mechanism that routes compartment decisions to the physically discriminative sequences will remove the predictable component of these errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Confusion matrices stratified by available sequences will show characteristic signatures matching contrast physics, and sequence-aware gating will reduce compartment confusion substantially more than uniform capacity increases.
why_important: Subregion accuracy drives radiotherapy dose painting and response assessment, and the fix requires understanding rather than data collection.
why_possibly_novel: Subregion segmentation is heavily benchmarked; error-physics analysis linking confusion types to sequence reliance with an architectural consequence appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Analyze per-sequence ablation effects on compartment confusions in trained models, verify predicted signatures, then implement gating and compare against parameter-matched baselines.
main_risk: Confusions may be dominated by label noise in subregion annotations rather than model physics, dissolving the pattern.
community_default_belief: Subregion errors are a data-scale problem that larger multi-sequence datasets will fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the discriminative information exists in specific sequences and models dilute it by uniform fusion, the error is architectural misallocation, not information scarcity, and more data will not fix it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Sequence-dropout evaluation of one trained subregion model, checking whether compartment confusions spike when the physically discriminative sequence is removed as predicted.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Shape-texture recombination of common tumors as augmentation transfers segmentation ability to rare tumor types better than intensity augmentation.
problem: Rare tumor types have too few examples to train on, and models trained on common types fail on them for unclear reasons, leaving rare-disease patients underserved by segmentation tools.
core_hypothesis: Rare-type failures are driven by unseen shape-texture combinations rather than unseen elementary features, so recombining shapes and textures across common tumor examples covers the rare-type distribution combinatorially.
falsifiable_prediction: Recombination-augmented models will improve zero-shot segmentation of held-out rare tumor types substantially more than matched intensity-augmentation baselines, and the improvement will track the rare types' proximity to the recombined feature space.
why_important: Rare conditions collectively affect large patient populations, and a method that extends segmentation coverage without rare-type data changes what is deployable for them.
why_possibly_novel: Copy-paste and stylization exist separately; systematic shape-texture recombination targeted at rare-type generalization with held-out-type evaluation appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Hold out tumor types across datasets, train with recombination vs intensity augmentation on remaining types, and evaluate zero-shot transfer to the held-out types.
main_risk: Recombined examples may be anatomically implausible in location or context, teaching the model to segment impossible configurations without helping real rare types.
community_default_belief: Generalizing to rare tumor types requires collecting rare-type examples or few-shot adaptation; augmentation cannot bridge type-level gaps.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tumor appearance decomposes approximately into shape, texture, and context factors that networks learn separably, so the gap is combinatorial coverage rather than missing factors, which augmentation can supply.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate a common-type-trained model on one rare type, checking whether failures occur on cases whose shape and texture each occur separately in training; if failures look elementary rather than combinatorial, the premise breaks.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Joint conditioning on treatment metadata separates post-treatment change from recurrent tumor in follow-up segmentation.
problem: Follow-up scans mix treatment effects (scarring, necrosis, inflammation) with recurrence, and segmentation models trained on treatment-naive data label treatment change as tumor, undermining surveillance workflows.
core_hypothesis: Treatment metadata (modality, field or resection extent, time since treatment) is strongly informative about expected treatment-effect appearance, so conditioning segmentation on it resolves ambiguities that images alone underdetermine.
falsifiable_prediction: Metadata-conditioned models will reduce false tumor labels in treated regions substantially relative to image-only models, with the gain scaling with time-since-treatment informativeness, while untreated-case performance is unchanged.
why_important: Post-treatment surveillance is the highest-volume oncologic imaging use case, and false recurrence calls trigger costly and harmful interventions.
why_possibly_novel: Post-treatment imaging appearance is a known clinical challenge; explicit treatment-covariate conditioning of segmentation models with treated-region error endpoints appears underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble follow-up datasets with treatment records and recurrence adjudication, train conditioned vs unconditioned models, and evaluate treated-region false-positive and recurrence-sensitivity rates.
main_risk: Treatment metadata in real records is incomplete and heterogeneous, and models may learn shortcuts from metadata to outcome prevalence rather than appearance.
community_default_belief: Recurrence-vs-treatment-effect discrimination is an image-appearance problem to be solved with more labeled follow-up data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The image is genuinely ambiguous in many treated regions, and radiologists themselves resolve the ambiguity using the treatment history, which the model is currently denied.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compare error rates of an image-only model on treated vs untreated regions in one follow-up dataset; if treated regions are not disproportionately error-prone, the motivating gap is smaller than assumed.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Progressive coarse-to-fine streaming of segmentation results changes clinical usability more than reducing total inference time.
problem: Deployment engineering focuses on minimizing total segmentation latency, while clinical workflow tolerance may depend more on when the first usable result appears than when the final one does.
core_hypothesis: Clinicians can begin verification and planning from a coarse mask delivered within seconds, so progressive refinement (coarse result immediately, details streamed) yields higher workflow acceptance than a faster but monolithic pipeline.
falsifiable_prediction: In a workflow study, progressive delivery will score higher on task-completion time and user acceptance than monolithic delivery even when its total compute time is longer, with the effect strongest in time-pressured settings like intraoperative use.
why_important: It reframes the deployment optimization target for the whole field, from FLOPs reduction to latency shaping, which is often much cheaper to achieve.
why_possibly_novel: Progressive rendering is standard in graphics and web engineering; measuring its clinical-workflow value for segmentation delivery appears absent from the literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a planning workstation to deliver identical final masks under monolithic vs progressive schedules, measure clinician task times and acceptance across a case mix, and analyze by time pressure.
main_risk: Coarse initial masks might anchor clinicians to early errors or erode trust when refinements visibly change contours mid-review.
community_default_belief: Reducing total inference time is the deployment optimization that matters; delivery schedule is an implementation detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human workflows pipeline naturally: verification of gross correctness and setup tasks can proceed on coarse output, so perceived latency is governed by time-to-first-usable-result, not time-to-completion.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Small timing pilot with a few users on a simulated review task under both delivery schedules; no perceived-latency difference undermines the premise cheaply.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: 3D medical segmentation on clinical hardware is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, so scheduling and layout optimizations beat quantization and pruning.
problem: Deployment optimization for hospital hardware reflexively applies compute-reduction techniques (quantization, pruning), assuming arithmetic throughput is the bottleneck for 3D segmentation workloads.
core_hypothesis: Sliding-window 3D inference with large feature maps is dominated by memory traffic on typical clinical GPUs and CPUs, so tiling, fusion, and precision-layout choices deliver larger wall-clock gains than reducing arithmetic operations.
falsifiable_prediction: Profiling across representative clinical hardware will show memory-bound roofline positioning for standard 3D pipelines, and bandwidth-targeted optimizations will yield larger latency reductions than aggressive quantization at matched accuracy.
why_important: Hospitals run on constrained shared hardware, and mis-targeted optimization wastes engineering budgets while leaving real latency gains unrealized.
why_possibly_novel: Roofline analysis is standard in HPC; a published characterization of where 3D medical segmentation actually sits on clinical-grade hardware, with optimization consequences, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Profile standard 3D segmentation pipelines on a matrix of clinical-representative devices, place them on rooflines, then implement bandwidth vs compute optimizations and compare wall-clock improvements.
main_risk: The conclusion may be strongly hardware-generation-dependent, aging quickly as clinical hardware refreshes.
community_default_belief: Quantization and pruning are the default efficiency tools for deploying segmentation networks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Those tools were developed for classification workloads with small activations; 3D segmentation activations are orders of magnitude larger relative to weights, inverting the compute-to-traffic ratio the tools assume.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One-day profiling of a standard pipeline on one clinical-grade GPU; if utilization shows compute-bound behavior, the thesis is dead on that hardware class.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Statistical process control on predicted-structure statistics gives hospitals label-free weekly monitoring of deployed segmentation models.
problem: Deployed models operate for years without accuracy measurement because labels stop after go-live, so degradations surface only through downstream incidents.
core_hypothesis: Population-level statistics of model outputs (volume distributions, laterality symmetry, per-structure confidence) are stable under correct operation and shift detectably under model-relevant input changes, supporting control-chart monitoring with actionable alarm thresholds.
falsifiable_prediction: Retrospective replay over archives containing known disruptive events (scanner swaps, protocol changes) will show control-chart alarms at those events with practical lead time and an acceptably low false-alarm rate during stable periods.
why_important: Regulators increasingly require post-market performance monitoring, and no label-free standard method exists; this would be an immediately adoptable compliance instrument.
why_possibly_novel: Drift monitoring is generic; a validated, segmentation-specific feature set with demonstrated alarm precision on real clinical archives appears unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the control-chart suite, replay multi-year archives from sites with documented equipment changes, and report alarm sensitivity and false-alarm rates against the documented event timeline.
main_risk: Case-mix drift (new referral patterns) may be statistically indistinguishable from model-relevant drift using output statistics alone.
community_default_belief: Meaningful model monitoring requires periodic labeled audits; output statistics are too confounded to be actionable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Anatomically-derived statistics like organ volume distributions are strongly constrained by physiology, so their drift is far more likely to reflect processing change than sudden population change, making the confound weaker than assumed.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Replay one archive year with one known scanner change; absence of any output-statistic shift at the change point undermines the approach immediately.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Quantify the decay rate of locked segmentation models under real protocol drift to give regulators an evidence-based revalidation interval.
problem: Regulatory frameworks favor locked models, implicitly assuming stationary performance, but nobody has measured how fast locked segmentation models actually decay in operational environments.
core_hypothesis: Locked models decay at measurable, site-dependent rates driven by acquisition drift, and the decay rate is predictable from the site's protocol-change cadence, enabling principled revalidation scheduling instead of arbitrary intervals.
falsifiable_prediction: Sparse longitudinal labeling of archived cases will reveal statistically significant accuracy decline at sites with frequent protocol changes and near-zero decline at stable sites, with decay rate correlating with a quantified drift index.
why_important: The locked-model doctrine is central to medical AI regulation; empirical decay curves would inform both regulatory policy and hospital procurement contracts.
why_possibly_novel: Dataset shift is well theorized; longitudinal, operationally grounded decay measurement of deployed-style locked segmentation models appears essentially undone in public literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze models trained on era-one data from longitudinal archives, evaluate on labeled samples from subsequent eras at multiple sites, and fit decay curves against drift indices computed from metadata.
main_risk: Retrospective archives may under-represent the drift dynamics of current scanner ecosystems, dating the conclusions.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Every component upstream of the model (scanners, reconstruction software, protocols) is updated continuously, so the deployment distribution provably moves while the model does not.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one frozen model on labeled cases sampled from two eras several years apart at one site; no measurable gap suggests decay is slower than the hypothesis needs.

one_line_idea: A property-based test suite for DICOM-to-tensor pipelines catches the preprocessing bugs that cause a disproportionate share of real-world segmentation failures.
problem: Anecdotally, many deployed segmentation failures stem not from models but from preprocessing edge cases (orientation flips, rescale slope errors, spacing misreads), yet this failure class is unmeasured and untested systematically.
core_hypothesis: The DICOM-to-tensor transformation has a small set of formal invariants (orientation consistency, physical-coordinate round-trips, intensity-scale preservation) whose automated property-based testing would catch most preprocessing-induced failures before deployment.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying the invariant suite to existing open-source medical imaging pipelines will surface real, reproducible bugs, and retrospective analysis of deployment incident reports will attribute a substantial fraction to invariant violations the suite would have caught.
why_important: Preprocessing failures are silent, catastrophic (segmenting a mirrored patient), and entirely preventable; a standard test suite is cheap field-wide infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: Property-based testing is mature in software engineering; its systematic application to medical imaging IO pipelines with an empirical failure taxonomy appears missing.

main_risk: If mature pipelines pass everything, the result is a reassurance rather than a discovery, though even that outcome has documentation value.

why_it_might_be_wrong: DICOM permits enormous metadata diversity (gantry tilt, variable spacing, multi-frame variants), and every library maintains hand-written special cases exactly where property-based testing historically finds bugs.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Generate a few hundred adversarial-but-valid synthetic series and run two popular pipelines; zero disagreements or violations weakens the motivating claim quickly.

one_line_idea: Defacing and anonymization steps measurably damage segmentation of structures near removed regions, and defacing-aware training recovers the loss.
problem: Privacy pipelines deface head scans and crop identifiable regions before research or vendor processing, but the collateral damage to segmentation of nearby structures is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation networks use context from subsequently-removed regions (facial structures, skin surface) more than assumed, so anonymization causes localized degradation near removal zones that training on defaced data largely repairs.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained on intact data will degrade significantly on defaced inputs for structures within a context radius of removed regions, while defacing-aware trained models will show minimal degradation, localizing the context dependence.
why_important: Nearly all shared neuroimaging data is defaced, and vendors receive anonymized data operationally; unrecognized degradation would affect research validity and clinical processing alike.
why_possibly_novel: Defacing effects have been studied for some morphometry tools; systematic analysis for modern deep segmentation with a training-side remedy appears sparse.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply standard defacing tools to labeled head MRI, evaluate intact-trained models on both versions with error maps stratified by distance to removed tissue, then retrain with defacing augmentation and re-evaluate.
main_risk: Effects may be trivially small for structures of clinical interest, rendering the finding a footnote.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks with large receptive fields consume whole-head context including skin and facial landmarks for spatial normalization cues, so removing them perturbs features far from the removal site.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate one pretrained head-MRI model on defaced versions of its test set; a near-zero delta everywhere ends the investigation cheaply.

one_line_idea: Identify which automatic quality metrics actually predict clinician editing time, and select models by edit-time-predictive metrics instead of Dice.
problem: Model selection optimizes Dice-style metrics, but the deployed cost function is clinician time spent editing contours, and the mapping between the two is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Edit time is driven by error topology (number of disconnected error regions, maximum deviation, slice span of errors) rather than error volume, so surface- and component-based metrics predict edit time well while overlap metrics predict it poorly.
falsifiable_prediction: Regression of logged edit times against candidate metrics will show component-count and worst-deviation metrics dominating Dice in explained variance, and reranking models by the predictive metric will change model selection decisions on real datasets.
why_important: If model selection is optimizing a metric weakly coupled to deployed cost, the field is systematically shipping the wrong checkpoints; fixing the selection criterion is free performance.
why_possibly_novel: Metric critiques are common; grounding a selection metric in empirically logged clinician edit times and demonstrating decision flips appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a contour-editing workstation, log edit times over a diverse case-model mix, fit predictive models from candidate metrics, and validate metric-based edit-time prediction on held-out clinicians.
main_risk: Edit time varies strongly across clinicians and tools, possibly swamping the metric signal with user variance.
community_default_belief: Higher-Dice models are less work for clinicians in proportion to their accuracy advantage.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A single large smooth error is fast to fix with modern editing tools, while many small scattered errors of equal total volume require slice-by-slice attention, so equal-Dice models can differ severalfold in editing cost.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Pilot with one clinician editing outputs of two equal-Dice models with different error topologies; similar edit times would falsify the topology-dominance premise.

one_line_idea: A quantified site-commissioning recipe: how many unlabeled scans and how few labeled cases a new site needs to safely adopt a segmentation model.
problem: New sites adopt segmentation models with ad hoc validation, having no evidence-based recipe for the minimal commissioning effort (unlabeled adaptation data plus labeled spot checks) that assures safe local performance.
core_hypothesis: Local performance after lightweight adaptation follows a predictable curve in the number of unlabeled adaptation scans and labeled verification cases, so a commissioning protocol with explicit stopping criteria can be derived and validated across sites.
falsifiable_prediction: Across held-out sites, the fitted commissioning curves will predict local performance within useful tolerance from the site's unlabeled-data statistics, and the derived minimal protocol will detect the unsafe sites in retrospective data.
why_important: Commissioning effort is the practical gatekeeper of clinical AI adoption; a validated minimal protocol lowers the barrier while raising safety consistency.
why_possibly_novel: Domain adaptation sample-complexity is studied theoretically; an empirically validated, deployment-facing commissioning protocol for medical segmentation appears missing.

main_risk: Curves may vary so much across model architectures and anatomies that no transferable protocol exists, only a methodology.

fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fit the curve on a subset of sites and predict performance on two held-out sites from unlabeled statistics alone; large prediction errors falsify protocol transferability early.

one_line_idea: Method rankings on saturated organ-segmentation benchmarks flip when re-evaluated with boundary metrics, changing which architectures the field believes are best.
problem: Large-organ Dice has saturated on popular benchmarks, and remaining method differences may live entirely in boundary quality that overlap metrics compress into invisibility.
core_hypothesis: Near the Dice ceiling, methods differ meaningfully in surface-distance and boundary-F1 terms, so re-scoring existing benchmark submissions with boundary metrics will reorder leaderboards and reveal that some celebrated methods are boundary-inferior.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating publicly available predictions or retrained implementations of leading methods with boundary metrics will produce statistically significant rank changes for a substantial fraction of method pairs whose Dice difference is within noise.
why_important: Benchmark rankings steer research investment and clinical procurement; if the ranking signal is metric-limited rather than method-limited, the field is drawing conclusions from noise.
why_possibly_novel: Metric shortcomings are documented; an actual systematic re-scoring study quantifying rank instability on saturated medical benchmarks appears not consolidated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce or obtain predictions from multiple leading methods on saturated benchmarks, compute boundary-metric leaderboards with confidence intervals via case bootstrap, and quantify rank correlation with the Dice ordering.
main_risk: Obtaining comparable predictions across methods requires substantial reproduction effort, and results might show rankings are stable after all, a useful but modest finding.
community_default_belief: Benchmark Dice differences, even small ones, reflect real and clinically relevant method differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For large structures Dice is mathematically insensitive to boundary displacement at the scale where surgical and radiotherapy consequences occur, so metric-invisible differences can be clinically decisive.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Re-score two methods with near-identical Dice using boundary metrics on one benchmark; identical boundary quality too would suggest saturation is genuine rather than metric-masked.

one_line_idea: Patient-level near-duplicates inside aggregated medical segmentation corpora inflate benchmark scores; fingerprint-based deduplication changes reported performance.
problem: As medical datasets get aggregated and re-released under different names, the same patients plausibly appear in both training and test collections, and no standard tooling audits this for volumetric data.
core_hypothesis: Anatomy is a biometric: patient-level duplicates and same-patient repeat scans across dataset boundaries can be detected via anatomical fingerprints, and removing them will measurably reduce cross-dataset evaluation scores of models trained on aggregated corpora.
falsifiable_prediction: Fingerprint auditing of popular aggregated corpora will identify cross-split same-patient pairs, and re-evaluating existing models on deduplicated test sets will show systematic score drops concentrated in models trained on the largest aggregations.
why_important: If contamination is nontrivial, a portion of reported progress in medical segmentation is measurement artifact, affecting scientific conclusions and vendor claims alike.
why_possibly_novel: Contamination auditing is active for language and natural-image data; anatomical-fingerprint deduplication for volumetric medical benchmarks appears largely undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Develop anatomical fingerprinting (bone or organ geometry embeddings), validate identification accuracy on known repeat-scan datasets, audit popular corpora pairs, and quantify score changes on cleaned test sets.
main_risk: Detected duplicate rates may be negligible, yielding a null audit, though publishing the audit tool retains value.
community_default_belief: Dataset-level provenance separation is sufficient to guarantee patient-level train-test separation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Public datasets are frequently derived from overlapping institutional archives and prior challenges, and nothing in current release practice checks patient identity across releases.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run fingerprint matching between two corpora suspected to share source institutions; zero high-confidence matches on a well-powered sample weakens the contamination concern.

one_line_idea: Replace mean Dice with failure-rate-at-threshold as the primary medical segmentation metric: it is more stable, more clinical, and reranks methods.
problem: Mean Dice aggregates a often-bimodal per-case distribution into one number, hiding the clinically decisive difference between a model that is uniformly decent and one that is usually excellent but occasionally catastrophic.
core_hypothesis: Per-case quality distributions of competing methods differ mainly in their failure tails, so tail-focused metrics (fraction of cases below an acceptability threshold) discriminate methods more reliably across seeds and datasets than mean Dice, and align better with clinical acceptability.
falsifiable_prediction: Across repeated trainings, failure-rate metrics will show higher rank stability than mean Dice for method comparisons, and method pairs judged equivalent by means will show significant failure-rate differences in a consistent direction.
why_important: Clinical safety is governed by worst cases, not averages; if the standard metric is blind to tails, method development is being steered away from what deployment needs.
why_possibly_novel: Distributional reporting is occasionally recommended; empirical demonstration that tail metrics are both more stable and decision-changing for medical segmentation appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrain representative method pairs multiple times on several datasets, compute mean-based and tail-based metrics per run, and compare inter-run ranking stability and decision concordance.
main_risk: Choosing acceptability thresholds is contestable, and results may be sensitive to that choice, inviting circularity critiques.
community_default_belief: Mean Dice with standard deviation is an adequate and comparable summary of segmentation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Means are efficient estimators for well-behaved distributions, but per-case medical segmentation quality is heavy-tailed and bimodal, exactly where means are least informative and least stable.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Plot per-case Dice distributions of two competing published methods on one dataset; unimodal, tail-free distributions would undercut the motivating premise directly.

one_line_idea: Leaderboard-standard post-processing like largest-component filtering trades away multifocal-disease sensitivity for benchmark points, and the trade is quantifiable.
problem: Post-processing heuristics tuned for benchmark metrics (largest-component keeping, hole filling) are applied universally, though their clinical effect on multifocal or atypical cases is opposite to their metric effect.
core_hypothesis: Largest-component filtering improves average benchmark scores because most benchmark cases are unifocal, while systematically deleting true disease in multifocal cases, so challenge-optimal post-processing is clinically harmful for a measurable case subset.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating standard post-processing across benchmarks will show aggregate-metric gains coexisting with severe lesion-recall losses confined to multifocal cases, and the net clinical utility under a cost model will favor disabling the heuristics for lesion tasks.
why_important: These heuristics are copied silently from challenge-winning pipelines into products; documenting their harm profile would change defaults in deployed systems.
why_possibly_novel: Individual papers mention post-processing choices; a systematic audit of the benchmark-vs-clinic divergence they induce appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several public pipelines, evaluate with and without their post-processing on multifocal-stratified test sets, reporting aggregate metrics alongside per-case lesion recall and a harm analysis.
main_risk: Modern pipelines may already gate such heuristics per task, making the critique partially historical.
community_default_belief: Standard post-processing is a harmless cleanup step that removes obvious false positives.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The heuristic encodes a unifocality prior that is false for exactly the metastatic and multifocal populations where segmentation tools carry the highest clinical stakes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Apply largest-component filtering to predictions on one multifocal dataset and count deleted true lesions; negligible deletions would blunt the critique immediately.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Measure how weakly Dice correlates with error in derived clinical measurements, and derive quality gates in measurement space instead of overlap space.
problem: Clinical decisions consume measurements derived from masks (volumes, diameters, dose-volume quantities), yet models are validated in overlap space with an unexamined assumption that overlap quality transfers to measurement quality.
core_hypothesis: The Dice-to-measurement-error mapping is weak and structure-dependent because spatially compensating errors preserve overlap statistics while corrupting derived quantities differently, so acceptance criteria must be set in measurement space per use case.
falsifiable_prediction: Across datasets and models, per-case Dice will explain only a modest share of variance in volume and diameter errors, with pairs of equal-Dice cases differing severalfold in measurement error, and measurement-space gates will disagree with Dice-based gates on a nontrivial case fraction.
why_important: Validation standards for regulatory clearance are being written now; if overlap thresholds do not bound measurement errors, current acceptance criteria are not protecting what clinicians actually use.
why_possibly_novel: The looseness of the coupling is occasionally remarked; a quantitative multi-task characterization with practical gate-setting consequences appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several structures and models, compute per-case Dice alongside derived-measurement errors, quantify explained variance and discordance rates, and compare accept-reject decisions under both gate types.
main_risk: For some simple structures the correlation may be strong, making the message structure-dependent and harder to summarize.
community_default_belief: A Dice threshold like 0.9 implies measurements derived from the mask are clinically reliable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dice is invariant to error direction and location, but volume error depends on signed imbalance and diameter error on worst-axis geometry, so the metric provably cannot bound either quantity tightly.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Scatter-plot per-case Dice against volume error for one organ and one model; a tight monotone relationship would refute the weak-coupling claim for that setting.

one_line_idea: A statistical-power audit of medical segmentation papers: typical test sizes cannot support the claimed method differences, and a bootstrap harness fixes the practice.
problem: Medical segmentation papers routinely claim superiority from small fixed test sets without power analysis, and the field lacks any norm for statistical sufficiency of segmentation comparisons.
core_hypothesis: Given observed per-case variance on common datasets, the minimal detectable Dice difference at standard test sizes is larger than most claimed improvements, implying that a substantial fraction of published deltas are statistically unsupported.
falsifiable_prediction: Computing minimal detectable effects from public per-case results will show typical claimed improvements falling below detectability thresholds for common test sizes, and bootstrap re-analysis of reproducible comparisons will fail to confirm a substantial fraction of published orderings.
why_important: If the evidentiary basis of method comparisons is systematically inadequate, the field's perceived progress ordering is partly noise, which matters for both science and clinical adoption choices.
why_possibly_novel: Statistical malpractice critiques exist in ML broadly; a segmentation-specific quantitative audit with released power-analysis tooling for the medical imaging community appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble per-case metric distributions from public challenges and reproducible papers, compute power curves for standard test sizes, and bootstrap-test a sample of published comparisons for confirmation rates.
main_risk: The audit critiques community practice and may face resistance; careful, non-adversarial framing and constructive tooling are essential to impact.
community_default_belief: A higher mean on the standard test split constitutes adequate evidence of method superiority.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-case segmentation metrics have high variance and strong inter-case correlation across methods, so small mean differences on tens of cases are well within resampling noise, a fact standard reporting never surfaces.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Bootstrap confidence intervals for the gap between two well-known methods on one public benchmark; if typical published gaps vastly exceed interval widths, the crisis framing is overstated.
