one_line_idea: Surface-distance metrics computed in voxel units versus physical millimeters materially change conclusions on anisotropic data, and the field conflates them.
problem: Evaluation code differs silently in whether distances are computed in voxel index space or physical space, which diverge exactly on the anisotropic clinical data where distance metrics matter most.
core_hypothesis: A meaningful fraction of published surface-distance results on anisotropic datasets are computed in voxel space or with incorrect spacing handling, and correcting the computation changes method comparisons and clinical-threshold conclusions.
falsifiable_prediction: Auditing public evaluation code will find implementations with unit inconsistencies, and re-computing published-style comparisons with correct physical-space metrics on anisotropic data will change effect sizes and some orderings beyond bootstrap noise.
why_important: Distance metrics feed clinical acceptability thresholds expressed in millimeters; unit confusion breaks the bridge between reported numbers and clinical meaning.
why_possibly_novel: Metric-implementation pitfalls are periodically discussed; a concrete audit quantifying the unit-handling problem and its effect on conclusions in medical segmentation appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Audit widely used evaluation implementations for spacing handling, construct anisotropic test cases with known analytic distances, and quantify discrepancies and their effect on real method comparisons.
main_risk: Major toolkits may prove correct, reducing the finding to edge cases in ad hoc research code, though standardization value remains.
community_default_belief: Published surface-distance numbers are computed consistently and are comparable across papers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Distance computation requires explicit spacing plumbing that differs across array libraries, and anisotropic data punishes any implementation that defaults to index space, an easy and silent mistake.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Run three popular evaluation implementations on one synthetic anisotropic case with a known distance; agreement with the analytic value everywhere would deflate the concern quickly.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Normalize segmentation scores by structure-specific achievable ceilings (inter-rater bands) to make performance comparable across structures and datasets.
problem: A Dice of 0.85 signifies excellence for some structures and failure for others, yet cross-structure and cross-dataset comparisons treat metric values as absolute, distorting priorities and progress claims.
core_hypothesis: Expressing performance as the fraction of the gap closed between a trivial baseline and the structure-specific inter-rater ceiling yields a normalized score that is comparable across structures and reveals which tasks are actually solved versus underperformed.
falsifiable_prediction: Normalized re-scoring of existing results will reorder the apparent difficulty ranking of structures, identifying structures currently believed hard that are near their ceiling and structures believed easy that sit far below theirs.
why_important: Research investment and clinical trust both follow perceived performance; a ceiling-aware score redirects attention to where genuine headroom exists.
why_possibly_novel: Inter-rater ceilings are reported in isolated studies; a systematic normalized-score framework applied across public benchmarks appears not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect or measure inter-rater bands for structures across multi-rater datasets, define the normalized score, re-score public results, and analyze how difficulty orderings and progress narratives change.
main_risk: Ceiling estimates depend on rater cohorts and protocols, and disputed ceilings would propagate disputes into every normalized number.
community_default_belief: Metric values are comparable enough across tasks that a universal quality intuition (Dice above 0.9 is good) is serviceable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The achievable ceiling varies enormously with boundary ambiguity and structure size; without normalization the same number encodes opposite messages about model quality on different structures.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute ceilings from two multi-rater datasets and check whether normalized scores actually change the structure difficulty ordering; if orderings are preserved, the added machinery is unnecessary.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: In interactive medical segmentation, guiding users where to click next matters more than improving the model that consumes the clicks.
problem: Interactive segmentation research optimizes model response to given prompts, while real users waste their interaction budget on uninformative click placements, a factor no benchmark measures.
core_hypothesis: The marginal value of a click varies enormously with placement, and a guidance overlay that suggests maximal-expected-correction locations will improve the accuracy-per-click curve more than upgrading the underlying model generation.
falsifiable_prediction: In user studies with a fixed model, guidance will improve accuracy-at-k-clicks substantially over unguided interaction, exceeding the improvement from swapping to a stronger model without guidance.
why_important: Interactive tools are the near-term deployment reality of medical segmentation, and interaction efficiency determines their clinical viability more than benchmark accuracy.
why_possibly_novel: Optimal prompt simulation exists in training protocols; delivering placement guidance to human users and measuring the human-in-the-loop efficiency gain appears largely unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a guidance overlay from expected-error maps, run counterbalanced user sessions (guided vs unguided, weak vs strong model), and compare accuracy-per-click curves across conditions.
main_risk: Users may find guidance intrusive or override it, and human study variance may require larger cohorts than anticipated.
community_default_belief: Better interactive models are the path to better interactive segmentation; users will naturally click where correction is needed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Users see only the current contour, not the model's uncertainty structure, so their click placement is systematically suboptimal in ways the model itself can predict and correct.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Simulate user clicks (random-on-error vs oracle placement) with one model; a small gap between placement policies would mean guidance has little headroom even in principle.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Editing three orthogonal slices and propagating in 3D beats iterative clicking for volumetric correction workflows.
problem: Interactive 3D segmentation tools inherit click-based interaction from 2D natural-image tools, though volumetric correction may be better served by dense edits on a few well-chosen planes.
core_hypothesis: Clinician edits on three orthogonal planes carry more constraint information per minute than sequences of isolated clicks, so plane-edit-plus-propagation reaches acceptable 3D contours faster than click-iterate loops.
falsifiable_prediction: In timed correction tasks, the plane-editing workflow will reach the acceptability threshold in less total time than click-based interaction for most 3D structures, with click-based winning only on small blob-like lesions.
why_important: Correction workflow design determines the real labor cost of semi-automated contouring in radiotherapy and surgery planning, a daily activity in every treatment center.
why_possibly_novel: Both interaction styles exist in tools; a controlled human-time comparison with structure-type stratification and a propagation model tuned for dense planar edits appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both workflows over the same base model, run counterbalanced timed sessions with clinicians across structure types, and compare time-to-acceptable-contour distributions.
main_risk: Results may hinge on propagation quality, entangling the interaction-paradigm question with implementation strength.
community_default_belief: Click-based interaction, proven in natural-image tools, is the right interface for 3D medical correction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A click conveys a point constraint while a plane edit conveys a dense curve with orientation information; per unit of user time, dense constraints propagate far more correction through a 3D volume.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Simulation study replacing human edits with synthetic plane-edits vs equal-time click budgets on one dataset; if clicks dominate in simulation, the human study is unnecessary.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Persist user corrections into a per-patient adapter so the model never repeats the same mistake across slices and timepoints.
problem: Interactive tools treat each correction as transient prompt context, forcing clinicians to repeat equivalent corrections across adjacent slices and follow-up studies of the same patient.
core_hypothesis: Corrections encode patient-specific appearance deviations that a lightweight per-patient adapter can absorb online, reducing repeated-correction burden without degrading the base model or other patients.
falsifiable_prediction: With adapter persistence, the number of corrections needed on subsequent slices and follow-up scans of the same patient will drop substantially relative to stateless interaction, with no measurable base-model drift.
why_important: Repeated correction of the same error is the most-cited frustration with assisted contouring, and follow-up imaging of the same patient is the dominant oncology workflow.
why_possibly_novel: Online adaptation and interactive segmentation exist separately; patient-scoped persistent adaptation with safety isolation appears unexplored as a workflow primitive.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate sequential slice and timepoint correction sessions on longitudinal datasets, comparing correction counts under stateless vs adapter-persistent interaction, and audit adapter effects on held-out patients.
main_risk: Adapters trained on a few corrections may overfit and corrupt predictions elsewhere in the same patient, requiring careful regularization to stay safe.
community_default_belief: Model weights must remain frozen in deployment; corrections are ephemeral interaction data, not training signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Patient-scoped adapters sidestep the regulatory concern because their blast radius is one patient's session, while capturing exactly the recurring patient-specific information stateless designs discard.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Simulate correction propagation on one longitudinal case series; if slice-to-slice correction repetition is already rare for modern models, the pain point is smaller than assumed.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Automation bias in contour review: clinicians accept plausible-but-wrong AI boundaries, and deliberate uncertainty highlighting restores scrutiny where it matters.
problem: As segmentation models produce smoother, more confident-looking contours, reviewers may scrutinize them less, so residual errors could survive review at higher rates than with visibly imperfect earlier tools.
core_hypothesis: Reviewer scrutiny is driven by visual signals of imperfection rather than true error likelihood, so polished wrong contours pass review more often than rough wrong contours of equal error magnitude, and targeted uncertainty highlighting counteracts the bias.
falsifiable_prediction: In reader studies with seeded errors, acceptance rates of erroneous contours will be significantly higher for smooth renderings than rough ones at matched error, and uncertainty highlighting will selectively recover error detection on the smooth condition.
why_important: The safety case for human-in-the-loop deployment rests on effective review; if polish defeats scrutiny, better-looking models can paradoxically raise clinical risk.
why_possibly_novel: Automation bias is documented in radiology decision support; its dependence on contour rendering quality in segmentation review, with a mitigation, appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reader study crossing error presence, contour smoothness, and highlighting condition, measuring acceptance and detection rates with clinicians blinded to the manipulation.
main_risk: Human-subject logistics and the difficulty of seeding realistic errors without detection artifacts complicate execution.
community_default_belief: Expert review is a robust safety net that catches meaningful model errors regardless of output styling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Perceptual trust heuristics track surface quality cues; polished outputs remove exactly the cues that historically triggered expert scrutiny, without removing the errors.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Small pilot comparing acceptance of matched-error smooth vs rough contours in a handful of reviewers; no acceptance difference would undercut the bias premise before a full study.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Single clicks are ambiguous between nested anatomical structures; multi-hypothesis output plus one disambiguating click saves interaction budget.
problem: A click inside a tumor is equally consistent with the enhancing core, the whole tumor, or tumor-plus-edema, and current interactive models silently commit to one interpretation, forcing corrective interaction.
core_hypothesis: Explicitly returning the small set of nested plausible targets and letting the user select once resolves scale ambiguity cheaper than iterative boundary correction of a wrongly scoped initial mask.
falsifiable_prediction: On nested-structure tasks, the multi-hypothesis workflow will reach target contours with fewer total interactions than single-output baselines, with the advantage proportional to the measured scale ambiguity of the prompt location.
why_important: Nested targets are the norm in oncology imaging, so scale ambiguity is a structural inefficiency of click-based medical interaction rather than an edge case.
why_possibly_novel: Ambiguity-aware interactive segmentation exists for natural images; grounding hypothesis sets in anatomical containment hierarchies and quantifying interaction savings in medical nested structures appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a hypothesis-set model on nested-label datasets, simulate and then user-test interaction sessions against single-output baselines, counting interactions to criterion per target scope.
main_risk: Presenting multiple contours may cognitively burden users enough to offset the interaction savings.
community_default_belief: Iterative refinement handles ambiguity adequately; a good model plus more clicks converges to the intended target.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Refinement clicks correct boundaries locally but are an inefficient channel for communicating a global scope decision the user already knows and could state in one action.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure how often single-click prompts on nested datasets yield wrong-scope initial masks with an existing model; low wrong-scope rates would deflate the problem.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Constrained test-time personalization: a few gradient steps on user scribbles, restricted to normalization parameters, safely adapts segmentation per case.
problem: Per-case fine-tuning on user input could fix systematic local failures, but unconstrained test-time optimization risks unpredictable global changes, which is unacceptable in clinical use.
core_hypothesis: Restricting test-time gradient updates to normalization and small adapter parameters yields the local correction benefits of per-case fine-tuning while provably bounding output changes away from user-annotated regions.
falsifiable_prediction: Constrained personalization will convert user scribbles into larger error reductions than prompt-conditioning baselines on hard cases, while far-region output drift stays within a small bound, unlike unconstrained fine-tuning which will show occasional catastrophic drift.
why_important: It defines a middle path between frozen models and risky test-time training, potentially compatible with regulatory expectations because the adaptation surface is small and characterizable.
why_possibly_novel: Test-time training and interactive segmentation both exist; the safety-bounded parameterization framing with drift guarantees as the central evaluation appears new for medical use.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On hard-case subsets, compare scribble-conditioned inference, unconstrained per-case fine-tuning, and constrained personalization, measuring annotated-region gains and unannotated-region drift distributions.
main_risk: Normalization-only updates may be too weak to fix the failures that matter, landing in a dead zone between safety and usefulness.
community_default_belief: Deployed model weights must never change at inference; all interactivity must flow through inputs and prompts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The prohibition targets unbounded weight changes; a tiny, bounded, per-case-discarded parameter delta has a categorically different risk profile that blanket policy does not actually address.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On a handful of failure cases, check whether normalization-only optimization on scribbles reduces error at all; if the parameterization is too weak even locally, the approach dies early.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Topology-preserving losses help mainly when labels are noisy, not clean: a conditions-of-benefit study for topological priors in medical segmentation.
problem: Topology-aware losses show inconsistent gains across papers, and the field lacks an account of the data conditions under which topological supervision actually pays off.
core_hypothesis: Topological priors act as regularizers against label noise and data scarcity rather than adding information on clean abundant data, so their benefit is predictable from label-noise level and training-set size.
falsifiable_prediction: In a factorial study over label-noise levels and dataset sizes, topology-loss gains will be near zero on clean-large regimes and grow monotonically with noise and scarcity, reconciling the conflicting literature.
why_important: Topology methods carry real implementation and compute cost; a validated conditions-of-benefit map tells practitioners when that cost buys anything.
why_possibly_novel: Topology losses are an active area; a systematic moderator analysis explaining when they help, rather than another method claiming uniform gains, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid over synthetic label corruption and training-set subsampling on tubular and organ datasets, training with and without topological losses, and fit gain as a function of the two moderators.
main_risk: Different topology-loss families may behave differently, requiring a broader method sample to support general claims.
community_default_belief: Topological correctness losses are generally beneficial additions for structures with known topology.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On clean data the labels already contain the topology, so the prior is redundant; its value should emerge exactly when supervision fails to specify the topology, namely under noise and scarcity.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two-cell experiment (clean-large vs noisy-small) with one topology loss on one dataset; equal gains in both cells contradict the moderator hypothesis immediately.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Differentiable inter-organ containment and adjacency penalties eliminate anatomically absurd multi-organ errors at negligible accuracy cost.
problem: Multi-organ models occasionally produce anatomically impossible outputs (organs inside other organs, disconnected fragments across body regions) that destroy clinical trust regardless of average accuracy.
core_hypothesis: A small library of pairwise spatial rules (containment, exclusion, adjacency) enforced as differentiable penalties during training removes the absurd-error class without measurable cost to standard metrics, because the rules only bind on already-wrong outputs.
falsifiable_prediction: Rule-trained models will show near-zero anatomically impossible outputs on stress-test sets where baselines produce them at measurable rates, with mean Dice unchanged within noise.
why_important: Absurd failures dominate clinician perception of AI reliability, so eliminating them buys deployment trust disproportionately to their frequency.
why_possibly_novel: Anatomical priors are an old theme; a minimal, auditable rule library with the explicit claim of zero accuracy cost and an absurd-error-rate endpoint appears not consolidated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Formalize rules from anatomy, train with and without penalties on multi-organ datasets, and evaluate absurd-error rates on out-of-distribution stress sets alongside standard metrics.
main_risk: Pathological and post-surgical anatomy genuinely violates textbook rules, and hard penalties could suppress correct outputs exactly on those cases.
community_default_belief: Enough training data teaches spatial relationships implicitly; explicit rules are redundant scaffolding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Implicit learning provides no guarantee on the failure tail, and the rare-but-absurd error class persists in practice precisely because it is too rare to dominate the training loss.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Count rule violations of an existing multi-organ model on a shifted dataset; a near-zero baseline violation rate would mean the problem is already solved implicitly.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Quantized shape codebooks constrain segmentation outputs to plausible anatomy, trading pathology sensitivity for shift robustness in a controllable, auditable way.
problem: Under acquisition shift, decoder outputs degrade into implausible shapes, while unconstrained flexibility is only truly needed for pathological deviations, suggesting an unexploited structured trade-off.
core_hypothesis: Decoding through a discrete codebook of plausible shape tokens learned from population anatomy makes outputs robust to input corruption, and a learned gating between codebook and free decoding recovers pathology sensitivity where evidence demands it.
falsifiable_prediction: Codebook-constrained models will degrade far more gracefully under synthetic and natural shift than free decoders on normal anatomy, fail measurably on pathology when ungated, and match free decoders everywhere once gated.
why_important: The robustness-flexibility dial is currently implicit and untunable; making it an explicit architectural control enables application-specific safety configuration and auditing.
why_possibly_novel: Shape priors and discrete latent spaces both exist; the explicit characterization of the robustness-sensitivity trade with a gating resolution for medical segmentation appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train free, codebook, and gated variants; evaluate degradation curves under graded corruption on normal cases and sensitivity on pathological cases, mapping the trade-off frontier.
main_risk: The codebook may be insufficiently expressive for genuine anatomical diversity across populations, hurting normal-case accuracy at baseline.
community_default_belief: Free-form dense decoders are necessary because medical targets, especially pathological ones, are too variable for constrained output spaces.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Normal anatomy occupies a compact, learnable shape manifold; unconstrained decoding pays for pathology flexibility with fragility on the majority of cases where that flexibility is unused.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fit a shape autoencoder on population masks and measure reconstruction of held-out normal anatomy; poor reconstruction kills the compact-manifold premise before segmentation experiments.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Bilateral symmetry as a free self-check: asymmetry between predicted paired structures flags segmentation failures without any labels.
problem: Failure detection for deployed segmentation needs label-free signals, and the strong statistical symmetry of paired anatomy (kidneys, lungs, hemispheres) is an unused invariant.
core_hypothesis: Model failures break predicted left-right statistical symmetry more often than true pathology does once normalized by population asymmetry distributions, so a symmetry-based score detects failures with useful precision as a standalone monitor.
falsifiable_prediction: On mixed test sets, the symmetry score will detect induced and natural model failures with high AUROC while flagging only a bounded fraction of genuinely asymmetric pathological cases, quantifying a usable operating point.
why_important: It adds a zero-training, zero-label safety monitor deployable alongside any model, complementing confidence-based approaches with an independent anatomical signal.
why_possibly_novel: Symmetry priors are used for augmentation and pathology detection; inverting them into a model-failure monitor with an explicit pathology-confound analysis appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute paired-structure asymmetry distributions from population data, score model outputs on datasets with known failures and known asymmetric pathology, and report the detection-vs-confound operating curve.
main_risk: Pathology-induced true asymmetry may overlap too heavily with failure-induced asymmetry, making the monitor unusable in exactly the diseased populations of interest.
community_default_belief: Failure detection requires model-derived uncertainty; anatomical heuristics are too crude to be reliable monitors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failure asymmetries have characteristic geometric signatures (fragmentation, volume collapse) that differ from disease asymmetries, and population-normalized scoring can separate the two distributions.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Score asymmetry on stored outputs of a model with documented failures against healthy controls; overlapping distributions end the idea in an afternoon.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: For vessels and airways, predict centerline-plus-radius first and rasterize masks second: connectivity-critical uses need tree-space learning, not voxel labeling.
problem: Voxel-wise segmentation of tubular structures produces breaks and fragments that ruin downstream uses (navigation planning, flow modeling) which need connected trees, and voxel metrics do not even measure this failure.
core_hypothesis: Learning in a centerline-and-radius representation matches the true geometry of tubular anatomy, yielding connected topology by construction and better downstream utility despite potentially lower voxel-overlap scores.
falsifiable_prediction: Tree-space models will substantially outperform voxel models on connected-fraction and path-existence metrics while possibly losing marginally on Dice, and downstream task success (simulated navigation completeness) will follow the connectivity metrics, not Dice.
why_important: Bronchoscopy planning, vascular interventions, and hemodynamic simulation all consume trees, and current pipelines patch voxel outputs with fragile heuristics to obtain them.
why_possibly_novel: Centerline extraction and tubular losses exist; committing the primary learned representation to tree space with downstream-utility endpoints, rather than post-processing voxel outputs, appears not the established paradigm.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched voxel-space and tree-space models on airway and vessel datasets, evaluate connectivity and downstream-proxy metrics alongside overlap metrics, and compare failure modes.
main_risk: Tree representations handle anomalous topology (occlusions, malformations, surgical alterations) poorly, exactly where clinical interest concentrates.
community_default_belief: Voxel segmentation with topology-aware post-processing is the practical approach for tubular structures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Post-processing cannot recover connections whose evidence the voxel model already discarded, whereas a tree-space learner allocates its capacity to exactly the connectivity decisions that matter.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Quantify how much connectivity repair post-processing achieves on one airway dataset; if repaired voxel outputs already reach near-perfect connected fractions, the representation change is unmotivated.

territory: Medical segmentation: organs/lesions/tumors, modality-specific challenges (CT/MRI/US/pathology), annotation scarcity, clinical deployment constraints
one_line_idea: Confidence-based routing between a learned segmenter and a classical atlas pipeline improves worst-case performance beyond either alone.
problem: Deep segmenters and atlas-based methods fail on nearly disjoint case types (atypical acquisitions vs atypical anatomy), yet deployments choose one paradigm and inherit its entire failure profile.
core_hypothesis: Because the failure distributions are complementary, a router using cheap per-case reliability signals for each method can select the better output per case, improving tail performance beyond either method and beyond naive ensembling.
falsifiable_prediction: Oracle routing will show large worst-decile gains over both methods, confirming complementarity, and a practical router using reliability features will capture a substantial fraction of the oracle gain, unlike output averaging which will capture little.
why_important: Worst-case performance governs clinical safety and regulatory acceptability, and routing exploits already-existing tools rather than requiring new model development.
why_possibly_novel: Hybrid atlas-network methods usually fuse outputs; explicit per-case routing driven by method-specific reliability estimation with tail-performance endpoints appears under-explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run both pipelines on multi-site data, verify failure complementarity, train a router on reliability features (registration quality, model confidence, input statistics), and evaluate tail metrics against singles and ensembles.
main_risk: If failure sets overlap more than hypothesized on modern data, routing headroom collapses and the study reduces to a negative complementarity result.
community_default_belief: Deep segmentation has superseded atlas methods; maintaining a classical pipeline alongside a network is pointless operational burden.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Atlas methods carry explicit anatomical priors that fail gracefully under acquisition shift where networks fail abruptly, so retiring them discards exactly the complementary robustness a safety-critical system wants.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Cross-tabulate per-case failures of one network and one atlas pipeline on a shared test set; weak complementarity in that table ends the routing idea immediately.
